activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
Charlie found the gown in the garment bag on her closet door, where her mother had hung it two weeks early, still creased from the package. She carried it downstairs and laid it across the kitchen table, smoothing the sleeves with the flat of her hand the way she'd seen the dry cleaner do.

"It's not black," said Gibson, who had come over ostensibly to return a calculator and had stayed for the hour it took to iron both their gowns. "It's like the color of a pond."

"It's not a pond. It's dark green." Kailyn was sitting on the counter eating cereal from the box, which she claimed was a graduation-week tradition she had just invented. "Charlie, your tassel is on the wrong side."

"That's next week's problem. This week's problem is that we walk out to that music and I don't know what it's called."

"Pomp and Circumstance," Gibson said. "Everyone knows that."

"I didn't, until Ms. Joshi played it in class on Tuesday." Charlie had liked the sound of it, actually, the way it moved slowly enough that you could imagine walking in time with it forever. She'd looked it up that night, half out of boredom, and something had snagged in her mind. "It's not even the real title. Elgar took it from Shakespeare."

Kailyn stopped chewing. "From where?"

"Othello. We read it junior year." Charlie could still picture the copy on Ms. Joshi's shelf, the spine cracked at Act Three. "There's a speech where Othello talks about the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."

"Glorious war," Gibson repeated, as though tasting it. "That's what we're graduating to?"

In May of junior year, Ms. Joshi had asked them to write about a decision they regretted, and Charlie had written three pages about quitting piano, which was true but easy, a regret she could hold up like a ticket that excused her from deeper inspection. What she had not written about was the November before, when her father had asked whether she wanted to apply to the conservatory prep program the way she'd once said she did, and she had said no so quickly that the word was out before the question had finished. She had told herself afterward that she was choosing freedom. Some nights she believed it. Tonight, ironing a gown for a ceremony she'd never once pictured as a child, she found she could hold both explanations at once without either one collapsing, and that this was not the same thing as knowing which was true.

"Ms. Joshi said you should be the one to give the student address," Kailyn said, tipping the last crumbs into her palm. "Did she tell you?"

"She asked. I said I'd think about it."

"You always say that."

"Because sometimes thinking is the answer."

Gibson held the iron suspended above the gown. "You could say something about the music. Like, nobody knows where it comes from, and then everyone finds out it's from a war speech, and that's us, we're walking out to borrowed words." He set the iron down, embarrassed, as though he'd revealed more of himself than intended. Charlie looked at him and felt something she didn't have a word for, a kind of effusive warmth that made her want to promise things she couldn't promise, that she would write to him from college, that nothing would thin out between them the way it thinned out between everyone, eventually.

"Or I could just say thank you and sit down."

"Or that."

She thought about Othello at the end of the play, asking to be remembered for how he loved, not wisely but too well, a man narrating his own exit. The graduates would file out under those borrowed notes, and nobody in the gymnasium would know their antiquity, their long road from a London stage through a composer's ear to a folding chair in a school gym, and the not-knowing would make the moment no less sincere. It might exhilarate her, actually, to stand at the podium and say the true origin out loud, to hand four hundred families a small dark fact to carry home with their punch and cookies. Or it might just make her mother's face go careful and disappointed, the way it did when Charlie said true things at holidays.

Kailyn hopped off the counter and held up Charlie's gown against her own, two shades of pond, and the clock over the stove said nine-forty.

"Try it on," Kailyn said. "Just once, before the real thing."

Charlie picked up the gown.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
Claire cracked the oven door with one hip, both hands full of bowl, and slid the tray of chicken onto the middle rack exactly the way Mr. Suzuki had shown them in September. The school cooking classroom smelled like browning butter and scorched ambition, and she intended for her part of it to be only the first thing. Thursday nights the room stayed open late for students who wanted to use the ovens, and tonight Claire was cooking dinner for her whole family, or the idea of dinner for her whole family, which her mother had described over text as "whatever you're making, make enough for four."

She was making a lemon orzo with roast chicken and a yoghurt sauce, because her father had once said, offhandedly, that it was the kind of thing you got in good restaurants. He'd said it two years ago about a dish in a city they'd visited for her sister's swim meet, and Claire had filed the sentence away the way other people filed away insults or lottery numbers. Tonight she'd carried bags of groceries on two buses, and she'd written the recipe out on an index card in her carefulst handwriting, and she'd told Alisha in chemistry that she was, quote, "basically a professional now."

"Basically a professional," Alisha repeated now, leaning against the counter beside her. "You burned garlic bread in October."

"The toaster was set by an anarchist," Claire said. "That's different."

Charity was at the far station making something with lentils, and she drifted over the way she did, holding a wooden spoon like a gavel. She read the index card upside down, which was one of her gifts. "Step four says whisk the eggs into the sauce. Where are your eggs?"

Claire looked at her mise, which was what she'd privately started calling the tidy row of ingredients on the counter: orzo in its measuring cup, lemon zest in a saucer, yoghurt, salt, the chicken already in the oven. At the end of the row, where the eggs should have been, there was a clean stretch of stainless steel, shining and empty and somehow smug about it.

"I had eggs," Claire said. "I remember picking them up. I remember the carton being cold."

"Did the carton come home with you, or did it stay in the store being cold?" Charity asked, and Alisha made a small pitying sound, and Claire dug through both grocery bags, then her backpack, then her memory, which offered her only the sensation of cold cardboard and not its actual location. The carton, she was fairly sure, was still sitting in her fridge at home, pristine and useless, twelve kilometres away at the exact moment the recipe needed it whisked into a sauce.

"What happens if you just skip them?" Alisha asked.

"The sauce won't set. It'll be lemon yoghurt soup with floating orzo." Claire stared into the middle distance, where her ambitions lived. "My dad will eat it and say it's interesting. He says everything is interesting. Last year he called a parking ticket interesting."

Mr. Suzuki was at his desk grading quizzes, and when she approached him he looked up with the laconic patience of a man who had watched four years of teenagers discover, mid-recipe, that they owned no cinnamon. She asked, in one breath, whether she could run to the corner store, whether four minutes round trip was possible, whether the chicken would be alone too long.

"You can go," he said. "Take the sauce off the heat first." That was all. He went back to his quizzes. Claire stood there for a second waiting for the rest of the sentence and then understood there wasn't one.

At the corner store she bought six eggs and stood in line behind a man buying forty scratch tickets, and she thought, with the special clarity of someone holding eggs she has already forgotten once, about what she'd gotten wrong. She'd liked the look of the tidy row, the saucers of zest, the measuring cups lined up like a photograph, and she'd mistaken the look of readiness for readiness itself. Charity would call it performing. Alisha, more gently, would call it being Claire. There was a word for the actual thing, she was sure, some term for setting out everything before you start, and she was equally sure Mr. Suzuki had said it once in September while she was drawing on her notes.

Charity was waiting outside the classroom door when she got back, arms crossed, wearing the expression of a person about to be right in a way she'd enjoy. "So. You learned something?"

"I learned that you're an egoist who feeds on my suffering," Claire said.

"Also that cooking has a word for not doing what you just did," Charity said. "Mise en place. It's French. It means putting in place, measuring and preparing everything before you start. Sylvie in my class has it tattooed on her wrist, which is a lot, but she's never once run out of eggs."

Inside, the chicken was fine, the saucepan was off the heat, and Alisha had taken the orzo off the burner and set the colander in the sink without being asked, which Claire decided to think of as an act of friendship rather than an indictment. She cracked two eggs into a bowl, whisked them with the yoghurt and lemon, and stirred the sauce back together over low heat until it thickened into something that looked, if you squinted and were feeling generous, like the dish from the restaurant.

Her father texted at six-fifteen: On our way. Smells good from here, which was impossible, and sweet, and very him. Claire packed the containers into a canvas bag, and Mr. Suzuki looked up from the last quiz and said, "Next time, eggs first."

"Eggs first," Claire agreed, and she wrote it at the top of the index card, above the lemon, above the orzo, in letters big enough that even she couldn't miss them.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The park had been transformed overnight, red lanterns strung between the oaks like a second, lower sky, and Sierra walked in behind her mother carrying a tray of oranges she was not supposed to drop. It was the first year the family association had held the Lunar New Year gathering in Miller Park instead of the restaurant banquet hall, and Sierra had spent the whole drive trying to decide whether that was an upgrade or a demotion. The answer, she suspected, depended on whether you were seventeen.

She found Petra by the folding table with the paper lanterns, wearing a coat the color of a fire hydrant and looking around with frank delight. "Okay, this is so much better than the chemistry review session I skipped," Petra said. "What is all this? Tell me everything."

"Mostly food and loud uncles," Sierra said, but she was scanning the crowd past Petra's shoulder, because she had a specific errand. Every year her grandmother distributed red envelopes, crisp bills folded inside red paper, to the children of the family, and this year Sierra did not know whether she was still in that number. Eighteen was coming in March. College was coming in August. Somewhere between those dates, she had begun to feel, a person probably aged out of lucky money.

"My mom says you get them until you're grown," her cousin Daisy offered when Sierra finally worked up the nerve to ask, but Daisy was nine and thought grown meant being able to reach the top shelf. Sierra wanted a more rigorous definition. She caught herself wanting to introspect on it, which was a word she'd picked up from a college essay guide and which her mother would have mocked without mercy, and she decided instead to gather data.

The data was ambiguous. Her cousin Raymond, twenty-two and married since October, was standing near the stage with his wife and was visibly not in the envelope line, though he had been first in it every year of Sierra's memory. Her cousin Amy, twenty, single, was in the line and had a red envelope in her hand and did not appear embarrassed about it. So it was not age. Sierra turned this over while the lion dancers assembled at the pavilion, two of them, one gold and one red, blinking their enormous eyes at the crowd.

"So what's the red for?" Petra asked, trailing her toward the tea stand. "Like the lanterns, the banners, everything. Is it just a color scheme?"

Sierra considered deferring to her mother, who was within shouting distance, but her mother explained things in a lecture format that could outlast the fireworks. "It's luck," Sierra said instead, picking her words carefully. "Red means good fortune. And keeping evil away. That's the whole idea. That's why the envelopes are red and not, I don't know, blue." Petra nodded as though a law of physics had been revealed to her, which was somehow flattering.

Mr. Sharma from the physics department was there with his daughter, of all people, buying sesame balls, and he waved Sierra over and asked whether the envelopes were still being handed out for his daughter, who had been given one last year by a student. "For kids," Sierra said. "And unmarried younger relatives. The families give them." Mr. Sharma said the word back to her, "red envelopes," counting them on his fingers like a man memorizing a formula, and Sierra realized, saying it aloud, that she had just recited her own answer. Unmarried younger relatives. Amy was in line. Raymond was not. It was not about being a grown-up in the way Sierra had been using the word all winter, the college-and-top-shelf way. It was about the other thing, the thing she was not anywhere close to.

She found Raymond by the tea stand anyway, because he was the one person who could confirm it. "Does it feel weird," she asked, "not getting one this year?"

"It felt weird in October," Raymond said, watching his wife take a photo of the gold lion. "Now it feels like I'm the one handing them out, so, different side of the table." He shrugged. "You've got a while, kid."

She had a while. She stood in the line with the nine-year-olds and the twelve-year-olds and Amy, who was twenty and unbothered, and when her grandmother reached her, the old woman pressed a red envelope into her hands and held Sierra's fingers closed around it for a moment, the paper smooth and stiff and warm from her coat pocket. "Still," her grandmother said, which in her clipped vernacular meant more than it said, and Sierra felt something turbid settle in her chest, a mixture she could not entirely separate, part relief and part the strange grief of being told you have not yet crossed a river you half wanted to cross.

She had planned, in the careful way she planned everything, to say something dignified about being nearly grown, and instead she said, "Thank you, Pó po," and put the envelope in her pocket with the oranges balanced on her arm. Then Petra appeared at her elbow, holding out her own red envelope with both hands like it was radioactive, eyes wide. "So the nice lady at the stage gave me one, because, apparently, she said I count as unmarried too."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: For US federal Direct Subsidized student loans, the government pays the interest while the student is in school; unsubsidized loans build interest during that time.
story:
Gabrielle spread the financial aid letter across Nolan's kitchen table and pinned its corner with the sugar bowl so it wouldn't curl. "They accepted me," she said. "Three of them did. This is the one I can actually afford, maybe."

Nolan sat down across from her with his cereal, which he'd been eating standing at the counter until she arrived. Outside, the August heat made the air above the road undulate, so the mailbox across the street seemed to waver and swim. Gabrielle kept smoothing the letter with her palm as though it might still change its mind.

"It's two loans," she said. "Same amount, near enough. But they're not the same, and I don't get why." She turned the page toward him and tapped two lines. "Subsidized Direct, and unsubsidized. That's what they're called, right there."

Nolan read the lines twice. He was a junior; this was supposed to be his problem next year, not now, but Gabrielle had been the one who stayed after chemistry to help him when he was failing, so when she'd texted that she needed a kitchen table and somebody stubborn, he'd said come over. His mother worked Saturdays until six, and the house was his until then.

"One of them says the government pays the interest while I'm in school," Gabrielle said slowly, following the words with her finger. "The subsidized one. And the other one, the unsubsidized, it builds interest during that time. While I'm in school. So it's growing all four years before I even start paying it." She looked up. "That's it? That's the whole difference?"

"That's the whole difference," Nolan said. "And it's a big one." He took the letter and held it under the window light. The subsidized loan would sit there, quiet, not breathing, while she was in classes. The other one would quietly get bigger every month she studied. He thought of the maple seed pods outside school, the ones that spun down and rooted anywhere, unasked.

He went and got his own notebook, the one where he'd been keeping his mower money. He'd been saving since March, twenty dollars a week from shelving groceries, and he'd noticed recently that the credit union statement showed the balance growing a little faster than his deposits alone could explain. Interest, working for him this time, patient and small. He wrote two columns for Gabrielle's loans and drew a line down between them, one side flat while she was enrolled, the other side inching upward. "So if you can only take one," he said, "the subsidized one costs less in the end, because it doesn't grow while you're studying. The other one starts owing more before you've even graduated."

"I thought there'd be some catch," Gabrielle said. "Some machination buried in the last page." She flipped to the back, found only repayment charts and a phone number. "Fine. Maybe it's just what it says it is."

"Take the subsidized," Nolan said. "And borrow less than they offer, if you can. I'm taking my own advice with the mower. Mr. Siddiqui offered to lend me the rest of what I need, no interest, just because his lawn looks terrible and he wants me to fix it. But I told him I'd rather save another month first. It's not that I don't trust him. It's that I want to get used to watching money grow before I get used to watching it shrink."

Gabrielle laughed, then got quiet. "I'm scared," she said. "Not of the classes. Of the number." She tapped the page. "And it's not even a rational thing, exactly. It's affective, like the fear is in my body somewhere before my head gets a vote."

"Then vote anyway," Nolan said. He slid the notebook toward her, the two columns and the rising line. "Look at it as a shape, not a number. One shape stays flat while you're in school. Pick that shape."

Gabrielle took the pen, circled the subsidized line, and folded the letter along the crease it had already worn soft. Then she reached over and stole a spoonful of his cereal, milk and all, and ate it like she was sealing something.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
Alexia had claimed the sunroom of her grandmother's house as a studio for the summer, and by the second week of August it looked the part: jars of brushes, a folding table scarred with old color, a portrait of her grandmother half-finished on the easel by the window. The face was done, patient and warm, but the background defeated her. She wanted the exact yellow of the kitchen curtains at noon, a yellow so bright it seemed to hum, and every mixture she made arrived somewhere duller than the one before.

She had started with cadmium yellow, which was close but flat. A dot of white made it chalky. A thread of orange warmed it and then dulled it. She kept adding, correcting one mistake with another, until the blob on her palette had gone the color of wet cardboard. She dipped her brush in and held it up to the curtain, and the gap between them was almost funny.

Gracie found her like that an hour later, having let herself in through the porch door the way she had since they were ten. "What happened to your paint?"

"I was making yellow," Alexia said. "Now I'm making mud."

Gracie leaned over the palette, chewing the straw of her iced tea. "You know it's not like light, right? My physics thing last term. It's subtractive. Each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so the more pigments you pile in, the more light gets eaten up. Mixing a bunch together goes dark and muddy, not toward white." She said it the way she said most things, offhand, as if everyone had noticed this years ago.

Alexia looked at her ruined pile, then at the curtain, and felt something rearrange itself. All summer she had been thinking of paint as though it were light itself, as though brightness could be accumulated, added up. But the pile was doing the opposite of what she wanted. The brightness wasn't in the mixture; it was in the light hitting the paint, and every new pigment she stirred in absorbed a little more of it.

"So all my fixing," she said slowly, "was subtracting."

"Basically you've been un-lighting it," Gracie said. She was being facetious, but Alexia didn't laugh, because the joke was true, and because it had implications beyond the palette. She thought of the essay she was supposed to write for a scholarship application, due in nine days, on a prompt about community. She had been piling sources into it the way she'd piled pigments: her grandmother's stories, a statistic about their neighborhood, a quote from a candidate she liked, another from one she didn't. Every addition had made the essay heavier and less like anything she actually believed. She'd told herself it was thoroughness. Sitting here, she could admit it was fear, the same fear that made her add orange when the yellow scared her by being too plain.

Outside, Mr. Saleh was watering his tomatoes through the fence, as he did every evening, and Alexia called to him through the screen. "Mr. Saleh, if you wanted to paint something bright, would you mix a lot of colors or a few?"

He considered the hose in his hand. "Few. My mother painted tiles. She said a bright color is one color that behaves." He went back to his tomatoes, and Alexia wrote that down on the back of a receipt, because it seemed like a sentence she would need later.

She scraped the mud off her palette into the trash and started over. Cadmium yellow, unmixed, straight from the tube. It went on louder and simpler than anything she had made all afternoon, and up against her grandmother's grey shawl in the portrait it did something strange: it made the shawl look softer and the whole painting look like a room someone actually lived in. Not the curtain's yellow, exactly. A cousin of it. She could live with a cousin.

"So the essay," Gracie said from the floor, where she was reading the draft and frowning at it. "You've got eight people's opinions in here and none of them are yours. It reads like you're trying not to disenfranchise anyone. Every viewpoint gets a vote and nobody gets a say."

"That's a horrible sentence."

"It's a true sentence."

Alexia took the pages from her, folded them once, and set them under the paint jars, where she kept things she wasn't ready to throw out. There was a smaller truth she could write instead, about the pharmacy on the corner and the summer it nearly closed, and what the block had done about it, and how her grandmother had kept the ledger in her kitchen drawer like a family solvency was the same thing as the neighborhood's. One story, one pigment. It would be harder to defend than a pile of citations, and it might fail, and it would at least be bright.

She picked up the brush again and cut a line of pure yellow along the windowsill in the painting. Gracie held the jar of tea up toward the light, studying it.

"What?" Alexia said.

"Nothing. I just think you found the color."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
Alexia had taped the tenth sheet to the kitchen wall beside the other nine, and from the doorway they looked, she had to admit, like evidence in a trial she was losing. Ten paintings of the maple in the backyard: three at dawn, four at dusk, two under overcast, one during the sleet in March that had come out mostly grey with scratches in it. The portfolio instructions, emailed in June by the art program she was applying to, required ten works organized around a single theme plus an artist's statement of three hundred words. She had the ten works. What she did not have was any conviction that repetition counted as a theme, or that the admissions committee would see diligence rather than a girl who could only draw one tree.

Said came over on Thursday with two iced coffees and no sympathy, which was why she had invited him. He stood in front of the wall with his cup sweating onto the linoleum and said nothing for a long enough time that she started to defend herself.

"They're different," she said. "The dawn ones are cold. The whole yard is blue except where the sun catches the top branches."

"Uh huh."

"The dusk ones are orange. It's a different tree, basically."

"Okay, so here's the thing." He set the cup down on the counter, carefully, the way he did when he was about to enjoy himself. "In art history last semester we did a whole unit on this. Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral, in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year. More than thirty. Of one church."

Alexia looked at the maple. Somewhere in her chest a knot she had been carrying since June loosened by half.

"Same building," Said said. "Different weather, basically. And they're famous."

"You're not making that up?"

"Mr. Szabó made us write an essay on two of them. I got a B minus, so I remember it well."

She sat down at the table with the statement draft she had abandoned, six false starts deep. If Monet's thirty cathedrals were a body of work and not a nervous breakdown, then her ten maples were a method. She could be exonerated, she thought, by a man dead a hundred years who had stood in a hotel window in Rouen doing what she was doing badly from her mother's kitchen. She wrote at the top of a fresh page: Light is the subject. The tree is only where the light lands.

Then she stopped, because that wasn't entirely honest, and she had promised herself the statement would not be something she'd cringe at in December. The tree was not only where the light landed. She had picked that maple because her grandfather planted it the year she was born, and because painting it felt like a conversation with someone who couldn't talk back. That was a different theme, a mushier one, and she couldn't decide whether to include it or whether it would make her sound like a greeting card.

Her phone buzzed on the table. Makenzie, from the bio program she was doing at the community college: "how's the phenotypic variation of your tree coming." Alexia typed back "explain" and got, in fragments, "observable traits, ok, it's a bio term, like how the same plant looks different in different conditions, jesus, take a joke." She laughed, which surprised her, and wrote it down anyway. A taxonomy, she thought, could be a theme too: she could sort the ten paintings into dawn, dusk, overcast, sleet, the way Makenzie sorted her seedlings, and the statement could be about the sorting rather than the sentiment. That was one way of thinking. The grandfather thing was another. The Monet fact sat between them like a bridge with no planks.

She tried saying both out loud while Said ate leftover rice from the fridge. "The work is about light, and light is a way of measuring time, and I chose this tree because it was planted when I was born, so measuring time on it is also about, I don't know, measuring myself." Said chewed. "That last part you could cut," he said. "Or keep it. Honestly it's your funeral." She kept a version of it, two sentences, hedged with I think, because she was not sure, and the statement that admitted uncertainty felt more like her than the one that didn't.

Her father came in from the yard with mud on his boots and an envelope from the septic contractor. He put his reading glasses on at the counter, and she watched his lips move slightly over the estimate. "The drain field runs right past the maple," he said finally. "Roots are in the lines. It's coming out next month." He said it the way he said everything practical, apologetic and immovable. Alexia looked at her ten paintings, at the dawn versions and the dusk versions and the one grey sleet, at a complete portfolio of a subject with a demolition date, and felt something she could not yet file under any heading she had. She got up, found her pencils, and went out to the yard while the light was still good.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
The restaurant smelled like garlic and floor bleach, and Payton stood at the host stand trying to look like someone who had worked in restaurants before. She hadn't. She'd babysat and tutored and sold her old saxophone, but a real job, with a schedule taped to a wall and her name on it, was new territory. The manager, a tired woman with a pen behind her ear, handed her a form and said, "Fill this out, and if your references check, you start Saturday." Just like that. Payton's hands were shaking so badly she had to grip the clipboard against the counter.

She stepped into a booth to write, and her phone buzzed: her cousin Marcus, texting from Missoula. My boss fired Doug today for basically nothing. Doug was still on probation so there's nothing he can do. Payton frowned. On probation? She typed back, What does that matter, bosses can fire anyone for any reason. That's what everyone said at school. It was what her mom said, too, whenever her mom complained about her supervisor.

Marcus answered before Payton finished the emergency contact line. Not here. I'm in Montana, remember? It's the one state where, after the probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire you. Payton read it twice. It sounded like one of those things people repeat without checking, like the one about pennies being illegal to melt. She was about to argue when a boy slid into the booth across from her, dark-haired, wearing the same hopeful interview clothes she was.

"Sameer," he said. "I'm applying too. Dish pit. You?" He nodded at her clipboard. Payton held it up: host stand, weekends. "Congrats," he said, and he meant it, which surprised her; she'd expected rivalry, the way their class competed for the same scholarships. He'd brought two pens, and when hers died halfway through the tax section, he passed her his backup without being asked.

"My cousin just told me something insane," she said. "He lives in Montana, and he says that after a probationary period there, an employer generally needs good cause to fire you." Sameer raised his eyebrows. "He said it's called the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, from 1987." She said the words carefully, testing them. "Montana is the only state like that, apparently. Everywhere else, at-will." She didn't actually know what at-will meant in any deep way, only that it was the phrase adults threw around to mean you could lose everything on a Friday.

Sameer leaned back. "My uncle got fired in Ohio for, like, no reason. Wrong attitude. That was the whole write-up." Payton looked down at her form, at the box asking if she was over eighteen, and something about the smallness of the boxes made the whole arrangement suddenly visible: she was signing into a world where, in her state, her new boss could end her employment because of a mood, a bad morning, nothing at all. She had walked in wanting the job with a simple, complete wanting, and now the wanting had grown complicated edges.

The manager came back and collected the clipboard, told Sameer he could start Monday, told Payton Saturday, nine a.m., nonslip shoes required. Payton thanked her and asked, quietly, whether there was a probationary period here. "Ninety days," the manager said, already walking away, "like everywhere." Ninety days, Payton thought, but ninety days of what protection afterward, here, in this state? She didn't ask that part. The question would have sounded like an accusation, and the woman had been kind to her, had looked at her references without sighing.

In the parking lot, Payton and Sameer stood by their cars while the evening transfigured the restaurant windows into gold rectangles, the dining room glowing from within like something worth guarding. Sameer said, "Text your cousin back. Ask him if Doug's going to be okay." Payton did, one-handed, leaning against the warm hood. Marcus replied fast: Doug's applying at the diner on Third. They know him there. Payton smiled at the screen. Some acumen about people, she was beginning to think, mattered more than knowing the rules, though she intended to learn the rules anyway, all of them, whichever state she ended up in.

She thought of texting Marcus a follow-up question about whether good cause was really as strong as it sounded, whether it held, whether it failed, but she pocketed the phone instead. Sameer was still standing there, holding his second pen out to her. "Keep it," he said. "For Saturday." She took it, and the two of them stood a moment longer in the amber light before driving off in opposite directions.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Deuteronomy 22:8 commands building a parapet around a flat roof so that no one falls, and Jewish tradition extends the rule to other hazards on one's property.
story:
Vincent set his laptop on the kitchen counter beside a mug of tea he had already let go cold and opened the debate packet to the resolution: whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life. The assignment, printed in Mr. Choi's cramped hand, required that the argument come from the text itself, not from what a commentator or a classmate felt about it, and Mr. Choi had circled the phrase twice. Vincent's father was at the sink washing lettuce, and beyond the window the neighbor's extension ladder still leaned against their garage, unattended since morning.

Mira arrived first, shaking rain off her jacket, carrying a folder thick enough to be a hazard in itself. She wanted to win. She had said so in the car, flatly, without apology: she needed the prize money from the regional round because her mother had hinted, in the careful way of mothers, that the piano lessons were becoming a strain. Lorelai came twenty minutes later with her shoes untied and a paper bag of apples, and she dropped into the chair across from Vincent like someone settling in for a long argument rather than a rehearsal.

"The easiest case is something absurd," Mira said, laying out her index cards in a fan. "Stoning, mixed fabrics, a rule nobody would defend now. We concede those and look reasonable."

"Except Mr. Choi said the text itself," Vincent said. He turned the laptop toward her. He had spent the evening before not writing his case but scrolling, and he had found something he had not expected, a line in Deuteronomy about rooftops. "Deuteronomy 22:8 commands building a parapet around a flat roof so that no one falls," he read aloud, "and Jewish tradition extends the rule to other hazards on one's property."

Lorelai stopped chewing her apple. "A railing law? In the Bible?"

"A parapet," Vincent said. "A low wall. Their roofs were flat because that's where people slept in the summer, so a guest could walk off the edge in the dark. The rule is about not letting your property hurt somebody who has no reason to expect it." He watched his father's hands pause over the lettuce, then resume.

"That's actually clean," Mira said, pulling a blank card toward her, though Vincent could see her deciding how to fold it into the case she had already built, the case about absurdity. "But one verse isn't a principle. You can't generalize from one verse, or the whole thing becomes cherry-picking."

"It's not cherry-picking if the tradition already generalized it before I did," Vincent said. "Rabbis extended it to a broken fence, an unstable wall, anything on your land that could hurt somebody. The question the verse asks is whose responsibility it is when someone gets hurt on your property, and it answers: yours, before the harm happens. That question didn't expire."

Lorelai had begun arranging apple slices along the edge of the table like a fence, and she nudged one over the edge and caught it. "Okay, but Mira's right that it cuts both ways. If you can update one rule into something modern, someone else can update all of them, and you can't control the direction. You could build a parapet or you could tear one down."

Vincent sat back. He had been aware, all week, that his own reasons for taking the religious side were not entirely presentable, that part of him wanted to believe a text could hold across three thousand years because it would mean something he could not name could also hold. He tried to introspect on it honestly and got only as far as admitting that his argument was stronger than his motives, which unsettled him more than losing would. "I don't think the verse gives you a whole ontology," he said finally. "It doesn't tell you what a law is or why God issues them. It gives you one case and a logic. Whether the logic travels is the part we have to argue, and I think we argue it works when the harm and the responsibility are the same shape. A roof and a fire escape. Not a roof and, I don't know, what you eat."

"That's a test, not a rule," Mira said, but she was writing it down.

While they argued, his father dried his hands and left the kitchen without comment, and through the window Vincent saw him cross the wet grass to the neighbor's driveway and move the extension ladder down onto its side, out of the reach of the neighbor's small sons. It was a somatic argument more than a verbal one, and Vincent noticed that his father did not look toward the window to see whether anyone was watching.

Lorelai stacked her apple slices back into their bag. "So we end on the ladder," she said. "The parapet is ancient, the ladder is now, the duty is the same. Let Mira make the concessions up front and you close with Deuteronomy. Mr. Choi wants the text, so give him the text and let him decide what it proves."

Mira read her new cards over once, squared them against the table, and slid them into the folder's front pocket, where they would be the first thing she saw. "Run it once, out loud," she said. "From the verse down. And Vincent, don't editorialize at the end. Read the line and stop."

Vincent stood, took a breath the way he would at the podium, and began: "When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if anyone should fall from it." Outside, the ladder lay flat on the wet driveway, and the kitchen smelled of lettuce and rain.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The fight started over a throw-in. Evan wanted it short, Douglas wanted it long, and by the time they reached the bench their voices had flattened into that tone Antoine knew from his parents, each word filed down to something that could cut. Mr. Dela Cruz stood with his arms crossed and let it run for eleven seconds, which he counted, because he counted everything, then sent them both to run the hill. That was the third argument in four practices, and the season was barely half over.

Antoine walked home through the park with his cleats knotted over one shoulder, the spikes pressing a constellation into his collarbone. He liked walking through the park at that hour, when the sprinklers came on and the light went the color of weak tea, but tonight he couldn't settle into it. In September the team had been easy with each other, almost ebullient, everyone laughing at everyone's jokes because nobody had played badly enough yet to stop laughing. Now October had done something to them. He tried to name it and couldn't.

At home his sister's psychology textbook lay open on the kitchen table where she'd abandoned it for her phone. He sat down to eat beside it and a heading caught his eye, mostly because the words looked like a typo. He read the page twice, then a third time, his sandwich going dry in his hand. Psychologist Bruce Tuckman had proposed, in 1965, that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming, and performing. He copied the four words onto the back of a receipt and put it in his sock.

At Thursday's practice he waited until the water break, then found Douglas alone by the fence, spraying water into his mouth and mostly onto his shirt. "Forming, storming, norming, performing," Antoine said. "Tuckman, 1965. Groups go through four stages."

"Is that a play?"

"It's a psychology thing. There's a stage called storming. That's this. This is storming."

Douglas lowered the bottle. "So we're supposed to be fighting?"

"I don't know if we're supposed to. It's normal. It's a stage." Antoine hadn't worked out the rest of it, the part about what came after, and it embarrassed him to be quoting something he only half understood. "After storming it goes to norming. Then performing."

"So we're not even at the good part yet."

"We're not."

Douglas squirted water at him, and Antoine let it hit his shin guard, which was as close to forgiveness as either of them got. But at the scrimmage that night Evan called for the ball in a voice still carrying the argument from Sunday, and Douglas deliberately didn't pass to him, and Mr. Dela Cruz blew the whistle so hard the sound seemed to leave a mark on the air. He didn't lambaste them, though. Antoine had expected a lecture and got silence instead, which was worse, and then laps, which was worst. Running the third one, Antoine passed Evan and said, quietly, "storming," and Evan glared at him like he'd invented the word to insult him personally.

The next morning Antoine found Evan at the park, juggling a ball against the rusted backstop where the tennis courts used to be. Antoine had gone there to think, which was a thing he'd only recently admitted to doing, and had been sitting on a bench considering what his sister would call the liminality of it all, the in-between-ness of being on a team that had stopped being new and not yet become anything else. Evan juggled with his eyes on the ball, not on Antoine, which was how Evan conducted all his sincere conversations.

"I looked it up," Evan said. "The Tuckman thing. It's real."

"It's real."

"Norming is where they figure out the rules, right. Who does what." He trapped the ball under his foot and finally looked over. "We don't have that. Everybody wants to be the one who scores."

Antoine didn't answer right away, because it was true and because saying so felt like breaking some code. "Maybe we have to lose first," he said. "Or maybe that's not it either. I don't actually know what makes a team go from one stage to the next. The book doesn't say. Or it says it somewhere I didn't read."

Evan kicked him the ball. "Show me the fake you did Saturday."

They worked on it until the sprinklers came on and soaked the far half of the court, and Antoine got the fake wrong four times and right once. When Douglas arrived, bag over his shoulder and a bag of oranges under his arm, he stood at the fence watching them with an expression Antoine couldn't read, then came in and took the ball without asking. He did the fake better than either of them. "Saturday," Evan said, "you take the long throw."

"I always took the long throw."

"I know," Evan said, and peeled an orange, and handed him half of it without looking at him, and Antoine stood there in the hiss of the sprinklers holding a piece of fruit he hadn't asked for, which was, he thought, probably not what Tuckman meant by norming, and might be closer than anything the book had to say.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: On a closed interval, a function's largest value can occur at an endpoint where the derivative is not zero, so the endpoints must be checked as well.
story:
The math club met on Thursdays in room 214, a milieu Peyton had come to think of as hers even though she'd only joined in September, and today the whiteboard still held Tuesday's leftover graph, a parabola fading toward the eraser's usual indifference. She set her quiz on the table in front of Cale before she even took off her coat. The red mark at the top said 78, which was not a catastrophe, except that the lost six points sat at the bottom of the page like a debt she couldn't name. "I found the maximum," she said. "He took marks off anyway."

Cale pulled the paper closer. "You got the critical point right. I remember this one. Profit function, zero to ten days."

"Days until the fundraiser." Courtney dropped into the chair across from them, opened a binder, and produced a calculator with a cracked screen. "Regionals are Saturday, by the way, in case anyone's forgotten that we have forty-eight hours to learn derivatives from scratch."

Peyton hadn't forgotten. What she had done, since Tuesday, was carry the quiz around in the front pocket of her backpack the way other people carried worry stones, taking it out on the bus, at lunch, once under her desk during chemistry. The function had been a polynomial, something like three times x squared minus twelve x plus thirty, defined on the closed interval from zero to ten, and she had taken the derivative, set it equal to zero, solved, and announced the value at that point as the maximum, full stop. Six times x minus twelve equals zero, so x equals two, so the answer was the profit at two days. She'd been so pleased with the algebra that she'd never looked anywhere else. Mr. Santos-Reyes had written, in red, a single word: endpoints?

"Maybe he just imputes carelessness to everyone," Cale said, sliding the quiz back. "You know how he is. You breathe wrong on a test and he decides you weren't thinking."

"He decides you weren't finishing," Courtney said. She was already writing the same function on her own paper, her handwriting torpid and enormous, each letter slumping into the next. "Which, honestly, you weren't. Look, you stopped at the middle. Watch." She evaluated the function at zero, wrote the number down, then evaluated it at ten, and Peyton saw it before Courtney's pen finished the arithmetic: the value at ten was larger. Larger than the value at her careful, correct, derivative-equal-to-zero point. The maximum on the whole interval was sitting at the far end, at the endpoint, where the derivative wasn't zero at all, where it was six times ten minus twelve, which was not zero, which was forty-eight, pointing onward.

"So the derivative doesn't even matter there," Peyton said slowly. She was reaching for it, the shape of the idea, the way the curve could just keep climbing until it hit the wall of the interval and stop at the wall, not at any peak. "The derivative zero thing only finds where the graph levels out inside. On a closed interval, the largest value can happen at an endpoint." She said it again, quieter, testing it. "So you have to check the endpoints too. Every time."

"Every time," Courtney said. "Even when the critical point looks perfect. Even when you're sure." She checked her watch. "Santos-Reyes said he'd open the gym for practice at four, which gives us one hour and one pot of coffee, in that order."

Mr. Santos-Reyes appeared in the doorway then, keys already in his hand, and asked if anyone had questions before they moved to the bigger tables. Peyton looked down at the quiz, at the red word she had resented for two days, and found she didn't resent it anymore, though something else hovered at the edge of her understanding, a question she couldn't quite phrase: how do you know, before you check, whether the answer lives in the middle or at the edge, or is checking the only knowing there is. She folded the paper in half and put it in her pocket instead of her backpack.

"One question," she said, following the others into the hall with her pen still behind her ear. "Saturday, if the problem says closed interval, do we get points off for stopping early, or just for being lucky?"

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In the United States, a conventional mortgage with a down payment below 20 percent usually requires private mortgage insurance, which protects the lender, not the buyer.
story:
Kayla had never been inside a house this empty, and she understood immediately that empty houses were louder than full ones, every footstep carrying through the rooms like a shout in a stairwell. The open house had a folding table near the door with a sign-in sheet and a bowl of mints, and a woman in a gray blazer was handing out laminated sheets that said PRICE REDUCED. Kayla took one and folded it into quarters.

"You're the first people under thirty all day," the woman said, brightly, as if this were a compliment rather than a diagnosis. Behind Kayla, her grandmother was still struggling with the screen door, and Milo was right behind her, holding his phone up like a badge.

"We're not buying," Milo said. "We're doing a field study. Kayla's aunt said this street was a good place to learn about the housing market."

"Well," the woman said, "you're the market, whether you like it or not. That's the sad part."

Kayla's cousin Shaelyn arrived eleven minutes later, flushed from the walk from the bus stop, carrying a folder of her own papers. Shaelyn was twenty-four and had just bought a condo across town, a fact she mentioned the way other people mentioned marathons they'd finished. "I came to see what ninety thousand less looks like," she said, prowling the kitchen, opening a cabinet and closing it. "Mine cost more than this and it's smaller. I'm either a genius or an idiot."

"Could be both," Milo said. He was crouched in the living room reading the laminated sheet, which listed the price, the taxes, and, in smaller type at the bottom, the words "estimated monthly payment," a number that looked, at first glance, like a typo.

Grandmother settled onto the window seat in the front room and refused, politely, to move. "I'll look at the light," she said. "That's all I need to look at. You children go count the closets." She turned her face toward the window, where the afternoon came in dusty and gold across the refinished floors.

It was Shaelyn's folder that started everything. She had spread her papers on the kitchen island, showing Kayla the difference between the listing price and what she actually paid every month, and there was one line Kayla couldn't place, a charge that didn't correspond to anything on the laminated sheet. "What's this part?" Kayla asked, tapping it. "It's not taxes, it's not the loan itself."

"That's the private mortgage insurance," Shaelyn said, wincing at the word insurance the way people wince at the dentist.

"I thought insurance was for you. Like, if something happens, they pay."

"Nope. I called and asked, because I couldn't believe it." Shaelyn flipped to a page with a highlighted paragraph. "I didn't have twenty percent for the down payment. I had about nine. So the lender required it. And it protects the lender, not me. I pay for it every month and I get nothing if everything goes wrong."

Milo looked up from his seat on the floor. "So the bank is worried you'll walk away, so you pay a fee so the bank won't have to worry, and the fee doesn't cover you at all."

"That's the whole industry," Shaelyn said. "Congratulations, you're an economist now."

"That's not economics," Milo said. "That's just a club where you pay the bouncer to protect the bouncer." Kayla laughed, and the woman in the gray blazer drifted closer, the way realtors apparently drifted toward laughter, and asked if they had questions. Her name was Ms. Halvorsen, though her nametag said only HALVORSEN in letters so large it felt like a warning.

"Everyone under thirty asks about the same thing eventually," Ms. Halvorsen said. She did not launch into any speech; instead she pointed at the kitchen island, at Shaelyn's highlighted paragraph, and said, "Yours or theirs?" and Shaelyn said "mine," and Ms. Halvorsen nodded like a doctor confirming a diagnosis everyone had already guessed.

Kayla stood there doing the arithmetic in the margin of the laminated sheet, and the arithmetic was grim, and then she did something she hadn't expected of herself: she stopped doing it. Her mother's voice, on the phone for years, had gone one direction, rent is thrown away, rent is paying someone else's mortgage, and Shaelyn's folder went the other, look what they charge you for not being rich already, and Kayla had always treated these as two separate arguments that you picked between like teams. But standing in a stranger's kitchen, she could hold both. Renting was money that bought you nothing permanent. Buying without enough money down cost you a monthly fee that bought you nothing at all. Both things were true and neither one told her what to do, and she was surprised how little that bothered her, and also how much.

"Rent is what you pay for flexibility," Shaelyn said, in a smaller voice, putting the folder away. "That's what I tell myself. Then I pay the insurance and I think, well, flexibility with a penalty. Everything has a penalty."

"Or a price," Kayla said. "Maybe a penalty is just a price you resent."

Grandmother called from the window seat before anyone could settle that. She had been listening, apparently, in the way she listened to everything, sideways and silent. "Kayla," she said. "Come look at this light while it lasts. It'll be gone in ten minutes and then you can go back to your numbers." Kayla crossed the front room and sat down on the seat beside her. The light was doing something to the far wall, laying a long bright stripe across the plaster, and through the window she could see Milo out on the lawn now, photographing the FOR SALE sign, and Shaelyn arguing cheerfully with Ms. Halvorsen about whether the basement counted as square footage.

"You want an answer," Grandmother said. It wasn't a question.

"I want to know if there's a right move. Rent, buy, save, whatever."

"There's a move you can live with," Grandmother said. "That's the most anyone gets." She patted the seat. "Your generation wants to expiate the sin of not owning a house by age thirty. Mine wanted to expiate the sin of not owning two. Shaelyn's out there making herself the apologist for a lender she'll never meet, paying its insurance out of loyalty to an idea of being grown up. You don't have to do either one."

Kayla watched the bright stripe creep up the wall. "I don't even know where I'll be in two years. I might be anywhere. I feel like everyone already knows their plan and I have this inchoate thing, this half-plan, save some amount, somehow, eventually."

"That's not half a plan," Grandmother said. "That's a whole plan with the numbers missing."

Milo banged on the window from outside, grinning, holding his phone up so they could see the screen: the FOR SALE sign with the price, and beneath it he'd typed, in the notes app, KAYLA'S FUTURE HOUSE?? with two question marks. She held up both thumbs, then turned one of them sideways, which was, she figured, the most honest answer she had. On the lawn Milo shouted something about the basement, and Shaelyn shouted back, "It counts if you count it," and Kayla laughed and went out the front door into the last of the light.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
Olivia arrived at the library ten minutes early with Jane Eyre under her arm and a sticky note marking the scene where Rochester first appears, thrown from his horse on the ice. She had promised Ms. Quinn a two-page analysis applying a critical lens, any lens, to a passage of her choosing, and she had spent the whole weekend unable to choose. Feminism came to her more easily; she had opinions about Bertha locked in the attic. But the Marxist material unsettled her in a way she wanted to hold on to, and she could not yet say why.

Anas was already at the table by the window, standing at the small whiteboard Ms. Quinn had left there for group work, marker uncapped. He had drawn a line down the middle. "Okay," he said. "Two columns. Tell me who goes where."

"Where how?"

"Owners and workers." He tapped the left column, then the right. "My dad explained it last night. In Marxist terms the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages." He wrote OWNERS across the top of one column and WORKERS across the other. "So sort them."

Olivia sat down slowly. "Rochester's an owner. Obviously. The man is rich enough to be a magistrate and half the county shows up when he wants company."

"He's a what?"

"A magistrate. It's in the book. He sits on the bench, which is another kind of owning, if you think about it." She took the marker from Anas and wrote Rochester's name under OWNERS, then hesitated. "Jane's a worker. She's a governess. She sells her labour."

"But it's educated labour," Anas said. "Does that count?"

"That's exactly the question." She wrote Jane's name in the right column anyway, then added a question mark beside it. "She teaches, which is work, but she also lives in the house, which blurs things."

Elianne arrived with two coffees and slid one across to Olivia. "I read your message," she said, pulling out her phone and reading from it. "'Ask Anas about the Marxist stuff, his dad's a union rep, he actually gets it.' Very flattering to be summoned as a source."

"You said you'd already done your lens," Olivia said.

"I did feminist, on Wide Sargasso Sea. My paragraph was basically one long complaint." Elianne leaned over the whiteboard. "Where's Bertha?"

Olivia's hand stilled. "Where does Bertha go?"

The three of them looked at the columns. Bertha Mason, confined to the third floor, produces nothing, owns nothing, is not permitted even the sale of her labour. Olivia wrote her name on the line between the two columns, half in each half.

"That's cheating," Anas said.

"That's the point," Olivia said, though she wasn't certain it was a point and not a failure. She sat down and pulled the book toward her, flipping to the passage where Rochester interviews Jane before hiring her, the questions about her accomplishments, her salary arranged, the terms set. She read a few lines aloud, her voice low because the librarian kept glancing over. "He buys her whole mind for fifteen pounds a year."

"Which lens is that?" Elianne asked. "Marxist or feminist?"

"Both, maybe. She's a woman and a worker and the second thing makes the first thing worse, or the first makes the second worse, I can't get the order right."

Elianne took out a pen and began writing on a napkin, then pushed it across. Olivia unfolded it like a message, which it was. In Elianne's looping hand it said: "You don't have to pick one. Ms. Quinn said a considered position, not a clean one." Olivia read it twice, then turned the napkin over and wrote underneath, "What about Bertha? She's neither owner nor worker. She's just removed." She pushed it back.

Elianne read it, nodded slowly, and wrote one more line before pocketing the napkin: "Then say that. Removed is a finding."

By the time the librarian announced the library would close in fifteen minutes, the whiteboard held Rochester and his class of owners on one side, Jane with her question mark on the other, and Bertha's name still straddling the divide. Olivia copied it all into her notebook exactly as it stood, question mark included, because the question mark now seemed like the truest thing on the board. Anas wiped everything clean with his sleeve while Elianne stacked the cups.

Walking out through the dark parking lot toward her mother's idling car, Olivia was already drafting the first sentence in her head: not an argument yet, more of a claim that she intended to test, that a governess in a house like Thornfield is paid wages for her mind and denied ownership of nearly everything else, and that a woman kept upstairs is denied even the wage. She got into the car, opened her notebook against the dashboard light, and wrote the first line.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
The coffee shop smelled of burnt milk and cinnamon, and Alexandre kept rearranging the sugar jar, the napkin dispenser, his own hands, as though the table could be propitiated into giving him composure. Deanna had texted that she was five minutes away, then three, then, oddly, seven, and he had spent each of those minutes rehearsing openings. A joke about the weather. A question about her essay on sentience in the machines unit, which Mr. Müller had assigned and which she had, apparently, torn apart in class while Alexandre sat in the back saying nothing. Nothing felt right. Everything felt like a line in a play he hadn't auditioned for.

When she came in, shaking rain off her jacket, the bell above the door rang twice, and he stood up so fast his chair scraped and a woman at the next table looked over. "Hey," Deanna said. "You look like you saw a ghost." She ordered a chai, waited for it, watched the barista steam the milk with an attention that seemed deliberate, as if she too needed a small task to survive the next hour.

They had seen the horror movie first, that was the plan, and Alexandre's heart was still not entirely his own. The film had been stupid and effective, a farmhouse, a basement, a thing that never fully appeared, and at one point Deanna had grabbed his forearm and left four small crescents there with her nails. He had liked it. He was almost sure he had liked it, the grabbing and the whole evening, but there was a splinter of doubt he couldn't locate precisely, something Aikam had said last week on the bus that kept surfacing like a coin in shallow water.

"Your chai," the barista announced, and Deanna carried it over and sat down across from him, close enough that he could see the rain still beaded in her hair.

"So," she said. "The movie."

"The movie," he agreed.

"My heart's still going, honestly." She put a hand flat against her sternum, a gesture so matter-of-fact it took him a second to understand she was reporting a pulse and not performing one. "It's weird, being scared does that. Makes everything feel bigger afterward."

That was when the coin came fully to the surface. Aikam, two rows behind him on the bus, scrolling his phone, had said: did you know about the bridge study? In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge. Alexandre had asked what that meant and Aikam had shrugged and said, that's for you to figure out, and gotten off at his stop. Alexandre had thought about it once that night and then not at all, until now, sitting across from a girl whose hand had left marks on his arm.

"Do you actually like me," he said, and then heard how it came out and corrected, "I mean. Sorry. There was this thing Aikam told me. This study, 1974, these two researchers, Dutton and Aron. Men who'd just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy one. Same interviewer. Different bridge."

Deanna's cup stopped halfway to her mouth. "So being scared made them think they liked her."

"Or they did like her. Or the fear and the liking got mixed up and they couldn't tell which was which." He was talking too fast, the way he did in Mr. Müller's class when he finally raised his hand, and he made himself slow down. "We just watched a horror movie. My heart's pounding. You grabbed my arm, I grabbed yours. I've been sitting here trying to work out whether I like you or whether I'm just still scared, and I can't fully tell, and it felt dishonest not to say that."

The café noise filled the pause: the grinder, a hiss of steam, someone's order called out. Deanna set the cup down without drinking.

"You're asking me to figure out my own feelings in real time," she said. "In front of you."

"I'm asking if it matters. If the pounding heart counts as liking or doesn't."

"Maybe it doesn't matter where it starts." She turned the cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "Maybe it matters what you do after."

He thought of his father, earlier that evening, standing at the door with the car keys, saying take the bus, the roads are bad, saying it in a voice that wanted to be helpful and landed as surveillance. Alexandre had propitiated him with a joke and escaped. He thought of Mr. Müller writing a question on the board on the first day of senior year, how do you know what you know, and the whole class going torpid in their seats, nobody willing to go first, Alexandre last of all. He had spent a year not going first.

Deanna was watching him. Outside, the rain had thickened, running silver down the black window, and the streetlight turned each drop into a small falling stitch of light. The moment stretched, and he let it, because hurrying it felt like another way of lying.

"Here's what I actually know," he said. "I liked you before tonight. In class, when you argued that a machine processing pain reports wasn't the same as a machine having pain, I liked you then. That was months ago, no bridge, no basement, no farmhouse. So whatever the pounding is, there's something underneath it that was already there."

"Okay," Deanna said.

"Okay as in you believe me, or okay as in let's move on?"

She laughed, finally drank her chai, and set the cup down with a small decisive click. "Okay as in, do you want to get out of here and walk somewhere? It's still raining, and I read that wrong-bridge study thing differently than you do anyway."

"How do you read it?"

She stood, pulling her jacket off the chair back, and said, "They still called."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
Savannah had chosen the same table in the public library every Saturday since September, the one by the window where the afternoon light came in sideways and fell across her laptop keyboard like a hand resting there. Today the light was the same and the table was the same and everything else had changed, because the email had arrived that morning: an admissions portal update, a status that read only "in review," and beneath it, a line inviting applicants to submit updated test scores if any became available. She had one more chance. The digital SAT was offered again in two weeks, and she had signed up that morning with her heart palpitating so hard she'd had to put the phone face-down on her bed and breathe into her cupped hands.

She had taken it once already, in the spring, and it had gone wrong in a way she still couldn't explain to anyone without sounding irrational. The math section had started easily, almost insultingly so, and then the second half had turned brutal, question after question she couldn't fully parse, and she had left the testing center convinced she'd failed. Then the score came back higher than any of her practice tests, and she'd spent a week wondering if the College Board had mixed up her file with someone else's.

"You're doing the thing again," Phillip said, dropping into the chair across from her with his own bag of books. He volunteered at the library on Saturdays, reshelving, and he had a way of appearing at her table mid-crisis as though summoned. "The staring-at-nothing thing. What is it now."

"The portal updated. They want updated scores if I have them. And I registered to retake it, and now I'm sitting here thinking, what if the spring score was a fluke, what if I go in and bomb it and they see the lower number." She turned the laptop toward him so he could see the screen, as though the gray status bar were evidence of something.

Phillip looked at it, then at her, and pushed the laptop gently back. "You never actually figured out why the spring felt so bad and wasn't. Did you."

She hadn't. She had filed it under luck and moved on, which was, she could admit now, unlike her. Savannah was the person who read the syllabus twice, who wanted to know the rules of any game before agreeing to play it. Somewhere in the spring she had walked into an exam whose rules she hadn't bothered to learn, and it had worked out, and she had let herself not think about it.

Phillip pulled a chair closer, and Kevin, arriving late with a coffee he wasn't technically allowed to have in the building, lowered himself into the third seat and said, "Are we doing the SAT panic? Is this the SAT panic?"

"It's the SAT panic," Phillip said. Then, to Savannah: "It's adaptive. The digital one. It switched over in March of last year. How you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second module."

"Sets it how?"

"Harder questions in module two means you did well in module one. That's why it felt brutal. You were getting a harder second math module because you'd earned it."

Savannah sat very still. Around them the library went on with its Saturday business, the checkout scanner beeping somewhere near the front, a toddler negotiating loudly with a parent over the picture books. She thought about walking out of the testing center in the spring, about texting her mother from the parking lot, I think I failed math, and about the score arriving eleven days later like a letter from a country she'd never visited. She had believed, all that time, that the exam had turned against her, when in fact it had turned toward her, had followed her upward like a path finding the mountain.

"So the panic is backwards," Kevin said. "The panic should be, it felt easy. If module two feels easy, that's the bad sign."

"That's not comforting," Savannah said. "That's worse. Now I can't trust how anything feels."

"You couldn't before either," Phillip said. "You just didn't know it."

She opened her practice book, the one with the blue cover she'd been avoiding for weeks, and looked at the first page of math drills without really reading them. There was an older way of thinking she'd inherited from somewhere, probably from her grandmother, who called exams "the great equalizer" and distrusted anything that adapted itself to the person taking it, anything that sized you up and chose your questions accordingly. Savannah had once written a history paper about the exams of an old theocracy across the world, where tests had been given to sort the faithful from the doubtful, and her grandmother had read it and said, see, that is what testing is for, sorting, and Savannah had argued with her for an entire holiday dinner, insisting that tests could be doors instead of gates. She had believed it with the impermeable confidence of a sixteen-year-old, before any of the doors had actually opened or closed on her.

And now. Now she could see both views at once, and neither fully won. The exam adapted, which meant it measured her, specifically, and there was something in that she found intimate and slightly unnerving, being read that closely by a machine. But it also meant the difficulty wasn't a verdict, it was a response, a conversation, and that was closer to her idea of a door than a gate. What stayed uncertain was the part she couldn't reason her way past: whether a higher number would matter at all to a committee that had already read her essay, her transcript, the short paragraph about her grandmother's garden that she'd rewritten nine times. She didn't know. She might never know.

"I'll do module one drills today," she said. "Then tomorrow the hard ones. The earned ones."

"There she is," Kevin said, and raised his contraband coffee an inch, a small toast.

Savannah pulled the book toward her, clicked her pen once, and started the timer.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
story:
The science lab smelled of ethanol and the ghost of somebody's burnt hair, and Ryan had been staring at the same diagram for twenty minutes. The unit test was Thursday. On the whiteboard Ms. Wijaya had drawn a fat twist of DNA and an arrow leading away from it toward a blob labeled ribosome, and between them a thin squiggle labeled mRNA, and Ryan understood none of it. Not the way he wanted to understand, anyway. He could memorize the words. He had already memorized the words. What he could not see was why any of it needed to exist.

Angad sat beside him copying the diagram in colored pen, blue for the DNA, red for the squiggle, entirely calm. "It's like the lantern slide thing," Angad said, not looking up. "You don't take the original out of the library. You make a copy and take the copy." Ryan said nothing, because the analogy felt close and wrong at once, and he could not yet say why. Mae leaned across the aisle and said the copy wasn't the whole library, it was one page of one book, which was closer, but still it explained the what and not the why. Ryan wanted the why. He had wanted it since he was nine and had taken apart a radio to find the tiny person inside and found instead a desert of solder.

Ms. Wijaya moved through the rows setting out the models, snap-together beads for bases, a plastic ladder that curled. When she reached their bench she only said, "Build it. Don't look at the board." Then she walked on, and Ryan resented her for it, a little, because building without knowing was like being handed a script in a language you couldn't read.

He built it anyway. He unzipped the plastic ladder, laid the two strands apart, and sat there holding beads. Angad reached over and snapped a bead onto one strand, then handed Ryan a different bead, and Ryan matched it, and they went up the ladder that way, one laying down, the other matching, quick and wordless. Halfway up, Ryan stopped. "Wait," he said. "What are we even making right now?" Angad said, "The copy. The working copy." Ryan looked at his hands, at the single strand growing between them, thinner than the ladder, single where the ladder was double. Something destabilized in him, the old memorized version of the unit sliding loose.

"It's not a copy of the whole thing," Ryan said slowly. "It's built off one strand. One side of the ladder." He turned the model over. "The cell keeps the original in the nucleus and sends this out. The DNA stays put." He looked up at Mae. "It's like the original stays in the vault and you take the transcript to the courtroom." Mae laughed, short and surprised. He did not know yet what did the building, what laid the beads down in the first place, and he said so out loud, honestly, because pretending would have ruined the part he did have. He found the label in the chapter later that night, alone at his kitchen table: RNA polymerase, the enzyme that read one strand and built the matching strand, and what it built was called messenger RNA, which carried the gene's instructions out. He read it three times, then set the book down and looked at his own hand, at the skin of it, and thought: every second, in there, copies being made and carried out and read. He did not feel enlightened. He felt slightly vertiginous, the way Mae's little brother probably felt when she told him the night sky was old light.

Here is what Mae saw, because Mae watched people the way other people watched weather. She saw Ryan come in Thursday with the model in his bag, unassembled again, and she saw him sit apart from Angad, who had made his own quieter discovery this week, that his parents were moving him to a school across the city in June. Mae had known since Tuesday. She watched Ryan rebuild the strand during the test's last minutes, not to check an answer but the way you touch a bruise, and she understood that what he'd learned had cost him his partnership, that the gain and the loss were the same event seen twice.

After the test she found him at the window with the plastic ladder. "Ms. Wijaya says you got the essay question almost perfect," she said. "Almost." He turned the ladder over in his hands.
