"Translation's still fog. I get the copy going out, but what happens at the end, at the ribosome, I can hold it for like a minute and then it goes." She thought that was the most perspicacious thing anyone had said all year, though she wouldn't use that word with him, not after the incident in English class. She also thought of Angad's empty seat next fall and did not say that either.

"You can build the rest of it with me," she said. "I mean the ribosome. We have all year." "We have until June," Ryan said, and it came out more bitter than he meant, and he saw her flinch, and he knew she had understood what he meant and that neither of them was going to name it. He held out one half of the ladder. "You take this strand. I'll build off it."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
Jasmine had been to the cemetery twice before, both times for people she could not quite picture, and she had expected the third visit to feel the same: an obligation observed at a polite distance. Instead the ground under her shoes felt newly real, newly permanent, because her grandmother was in it. She carried the Scrabble tile in her coat pocket, the wooden G that her grandmother had once held up like a queen's scepter after winning with "gruff," and she had not decided yet whether to leave it here or take it home. Lyric walked beside her, holding the umbrella they weren't using because the rain had stopped an hour ago, and Mr. Berg, who had been the grandmother's neighbor for thirty years, stood at the gate in his cemetery caretaker's windbreaker, waiting to show them where the stone would go.

"You can put flowers if you want," Mr. Berg said as they crossed the wet grass. "Or nothing. There's no rule about it." He said it the way he said most things, as a man who had watched hundreds of families make this walk and had long ago stopped assuming any two of them needed the same thing.

The plot was at the far edge, under a maple that had dropped its leaves early. Lyric set the umbrella down and brushed the grass clippings off the temporary marker, which had the name and the dates and nothing else, which seemed wrong to Jasmine, because her grandmother had been an autocrat of the kitchen and the card table, a woman who had opinions about everything, and now she was two lines of text. Jasmine knelt and pulled the tile from her pocket.

She held it over the earth, and then she didn't let go of it. Her hand just stayed where it was, hovering, and Lyric watched her without saying anything, which was why Jasmine had asked her to come instead of anyone else.

"Tony texted me this morning," Lyric said finally. "His grandpa, the one from March. He says he thinks something's wrong with him."

"Wrong how?"

"He's still going to school. He laughed at something in the cafeteria yesterday and then felt sick about it. He thinks he's doing the grief in the wrong order, like there's a checklist and he skipped his homework." Lyric pulled a blade of grass loose and split it down the middle. "He asked me if it hits you later. Like a delayed thing."

Jasmine sat back on her heels. Three nights ago she had been awake at two in the morning reading everything she could find, because that was what she did instead of crying, and she had landed on a study she kept returning to, a psychologist named George Bonanno who had followed bereaved people over time. She had read the page twice, then a third time, because it contradicted everything she had absorbed from television and from the pamphlet the funeral home had pressed into her mother's hands. "He found that resilience is common," she said now. "That's the actual word. Common. Most people. And there are no mandatory stages everyone has to pass through after a loss. Not in order, not ever, if it doesn't happen that way."

"So Tony's not broken."

"Tony's not broken." She turned the tile over in her fingers. "But it's not that simple either, because I read that and I still sat here for an hour last night trying to figure out whether I was allowed to feel okay." The wind came through the maple branches and, guiltily, it exhilarated her, the cold clean push of it, and she hated that it did, and then she hated that she hated it, and then she stopped, because the spiral was familiar now, a staircase she kept climbing in place.

She thought of her mother, who had cried at the funeral and not since, and her uncle, who had cried every day and told everyone at the reception that it was healthy, it was the process, as though his tears certified something the others' lacked. Both of them, she realized, were doing the same thing she and Tony were doing: checking their grief against an imagined standard and finding themselves either above or below it. There was something atavistic in the checking itself, some old instinct that loss must be paid for visibly, in the coin everyone could count. But the study said the currency wasn't standardized. It said people were stranger and more various than the script allowed.

"I keep thinking I should cry here," Jasmine said. "Today. At the actual place. Like it's the venue for it." She looked at the turned earth, the wreath already wilting at its edge. "And part of me thinks if I don't, it means she mattered less. And the other part thinks that's insane, because I've cried twice in the grocery store over her brand of coffee and once during a math test. It doesn't care about venues."

"So what are you doing with the tile?"

Jasmine looked at it a long moment. "I'm keeping it," she said. "She'd say leaving a perfectly good G in the ground is a wasted play." She closed her fist around it and stood, and her knees were wet and cold, and she let Lyric pull her up the last inch. Mr. Berg was waiting by the gate with his hands in his pockets, unhurried, prepared to stand there all afternoon if that was what anyone needed, prepared to leave the moment they were ready, and Jasmine texted Tony as they walked, one line: "You're doing it right. Call me tonight." Then she put the phone away and took Lyric's arm, and the tile sat warm in her pocket, going home.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts.
story:
Florence had taped her draft to the wall of the art room where the writing club met on Tuesdays, and now she stood in front of it with a red pen that Mr. Sokolov had left beside the fruit bowl on the supply table. The draft was six pages about Victorian diet reformers, and at the top, in his narrow handwriting, sat a single question: what is this paper actually arguing? She had read it four times since Monday, once out loud in the kitchen while her mother washed lettuce and pretended not to listen.

"Read me your thesis," Omar said from the floor, where he was sprawled with his own draft, a paper about city bike lanes that he claimed was going to change municipal policy forever.

"Middle-class Victorians believed that spicy food encouraged immoral behavior," she said. "That's my thesis."

"That's a fact, though." Omar squinted up at her. "They believed it. You found pamphlets."

"It's a good fact," said Noa, who was reticent until she wasn't, and when she wasn't, it came all at once. "I would read that fact. I would enjoy that fact."

Florence looked at the wall again. She had eleven index cards, a bibliography in alphabetical order, and footnotes that followed the style guide so exactly she had dreamed about punctuation. All of it was scaffolding around a claim that nobody on earth would dispute, because the pamphlets existed, and she had photographed them.

"So what's the difference between a fact and a thesis," she said, and she meant it as a complaint, but it came out as a question.

Omar turned a page. "My brother says a thesis has to be arguable. Like, a claim a reasonable person could dispute." He said it toward the ceiling, as if the fact were mildly obvious and slightly boring, which was his way of being generous with information.

Noa had changed her mind already; Florence could see it happen, the way Noa's chin lifted when an idea landed. "So a fact is something everyone already accepts," Noa said slowly, "and a thesis is the thing you have to convince them of." She picked up a marker and wrote ARGUE in the margin of her own draft, underlining it twice.

Mr. Sokolov came in with a thermos and two clementines and sat down at the far table without looking at anyone's paper, which was his version of trust. Florence took her draft off the wall and carried it to the window, where the October light came through the wire glass in rectangles, and she read her sixth paragraph, the one about the diet reformer who called pleasure at the table a hedonist's snare. She had buried it there, halfway down page four, as if ashamed of it: her real thought, that the reformers were not mostly concerned with health at all but with disciplining the bodies of people they considered careless.

From where Omar lay on the floor, he watched Florence stand at the window for a long minute, pen hanging from her fingers, then bend and write something at the top of page one with two hard strokes. She crossed out the old sentence entirely, the whole confident parade of it, and underneath wrote a shorter one, the kind that could be argued with, the kind a reasonable person might resist.

"What did you put?" Noa asked.

"Diet reform wasn't about food," Florence said. "It was about control." She looked at her own words. "I think. I'm not sure yet how far it goes."

"That's allowed?" Omar said, sitting up.

"It has to be," Florence said. "It's arguable."

Mr. Sokolov peeled a clementine and said nothing, though the smell of it crossed the room, sharp and sweet, and Noa got up to draw a new line through her own introduction, and Omar, deciding his bike lane paper was no longer going to change municipal policy forever, flipped to a blank page and began again.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
story:
The porch thermometer at her grandmother's house read eighty-nine degrees, but Noemie had claimed the attic anyway, because the attic had the good light and the box of art books her grandmother kept up there between the Christmas dishes. She was supposed to be choosing a theme. Ten artworks, one idea, an artist's statement, due to Mr. Kerr by the end of summer, and so far every page in her sketchbook was a drawing of her own face.

Tatiana came up the stairs with two glasses of iced tea and found her there, sweating over a page of self-portraits that all looked, to Noemie's eye, exactly the same. "These are good," Tatiana said, setting a glass on the floorboards. "But they're kind of identical. Like the same picture ten times in different shirts."

"I know." Noemie pushed the sketchbook away. "I wanted to do identity, and identity is my face, and now I have ten portraits of one bored teenager." She had been telling herself the sameness was a unifying principle. It was starting to feel more like a limit.

Tatiana crouched by the box of books and started pulling things out, mostly watercolor manuals and a biography of O'Keeffe with a cracked spine. Then she held up a softcover with a woman in a blonde wig on the cover, staring past the camera like she was being followed. "Look at this one. It's that photographer. She's doing herself as all these different people."

Noemie took the book. Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. She turned the pages slowly: the same woman as a frightened housewife, a hitchhiker, a girl in an office, a diva on a staircase, seventy black-and-white photographs in all, each one posed as a character from a movie that did not exist. The films were imaginary, the scenes invented whole. She had never heard of the series before, and the size of it startled her, the way one face could hold a hundred lives if you let it. "Seventy," she said. "She did seventy of these and none of them look the same."

"Because they're not self-portraits exactly," Tatiana said, peering over her shoulder. "They're, like, fake movie stills. Cindy Sherman, that's her name." Noemie ran her thumb along the edge of a page and felt something shift, a door she hadn't known was closed. If she stopped trying to show herself and started inventing characters instead, the theme could still be identity, hers and everybody's, but each picture could become somebody new. She could be a stranger at a bus stop, a bride in someone else's veil, the disaffected daughter at a dinner party she'd invented, the whole cast of a life she hadn't lived.

She worked through the afternoon while Tatiana read magazines downstairs and her grandmother puttered in the kitchen. Between sketches she caught herself worrying the idea from the other side. If every picture was a fiction, was she hiding behind it? Her grandmother, when Noemie came down for dinner and showed her three of the new drawings, studied them with her glasses on the end of her nose. "Which one is really you?" her grandmother asked.

"None of them," Noemie said. "Or all of them. I haven't decided."

"That sounds like a statement to me," her grandmother said, and went back to slicing tomatoes.

That night Noemie sat on the porch with a pen and tried to write the statement Mr. Kerr had asked for. She wrote a paragraph about how a self-portrait could be a lie that told the truth, and crossed it out. She wrote another about solipsism, about how everyone was trapped in their own head and pretending to be other people was the only exit, and crossed that out too, because it sounded like a philosophy paper and not like anything she actually believed at eight o'clock on a Tuesday. The truth was somewhere between the two and she did not yet have words for it. What she had was a stack of drawings of women who were not her, and a feeling, small but stubborn, that they knew something about her that her own reflection did not. It did not portend disaster, this not-knowing. It felt more like standing at the edge of a pool she had already decided to jump into.

Tatiana texted at ten: did you finish the statement. No, Noemie wrote back. But I have eight characters and two to go. She carried the sketchbook up to the attic, where the lamp was still on and the Sherman book lay open on the cot. She turned to the last page, the woman on the staircase looking back over her shoulder at nothing Noemie could see, and then she set the book aside, opened to a fresh page, and began to draw the ninth stranger.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
The canoe tipped on the third morning, and by the fourth everyone at the dock knew whose fault it was. Ali had leaned out to film the heron, Gavin had shouted, and the boat had gone over in shallow green water, taking two phones and a dry bag of maps with it. Nobody blamed Ali out loud. They just got quiet around him, and the quiet was worse. Gavin, who was senior camper that week and responsible for reporting each group's progress to Mr. Rahimi, found himself rehearsing sentences all through lunch: you cost us the maps, you never think, you ruined the whole portage plan. Each one felt true and each one felt like throwing a rock.

Kelly-Anne sat down beside him on the picnic table with her sandwich and her battered paperback, the one she read every summer. She was the only person at camp who looked forward to the debrief sessions, because, she said once, she wanted to be a family therapist and this was free practice. "You're going to talk to him," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I have to write it up for Rahimi anyway," Gavin said. "Six people lost a day of paddling because of one person's stunt."

"Fine. Say that to him, then. Say exactly that, first, out loud, and see how his face looks." She turned a page. "Or you could do the other thing."

"What other thing."

"I-messages." She tapped the book's cover. "This guy Thomas Gordon, a psychologist, came up with them back in the sixties. You say how it went for you instead of what the other person did. Like, I felt stuck when the slides came in late. That's his actual example, more or less. It raises the problem without blaming." She said it lightly, one camper to another, and went back to reading, leaving Gavin with the odd sensation that a door had been described to him rather than opened.

He walked the shoreline trail that evening to think it through, and the two ways of framing the thing argued in him the whole way. One voice said the blunt version was more honest, that softening language was a kind of lying, that Ali should feel the weight of what he'd done. The other voice said the blunt version wasn't really about honesty at all; it was about the pleasure of being right, and Kelly-Anne's method was the harder, more honest one, because it made him say what had actually happened inside him. His heart palpitated a little as he tested sentences aloud to the water, which he supposed was a sign that the exercise was not merely an etiquette trick. He had felt stranded on the shore with no maps and six people watching him to decide what to do next. That was true and specific and it contained no verdict on Ali's character. Whether it would actually change anything, he honestly did not know, and he let that not-knowing sit beside him on the bench like a second pack he had agreed to carry.

He found Ali at the fire pit, alone, turning a stick in the coals. Ali's own want had been obvious all week: he was building a highlight reel for his application to some outdoor film program, and the heron footage was going to be the centerpiece, the one shot he'd been telling everyone about since June. He had lost his own camera in the spill. Nobody had mentioned that part.

"I'm doing the debrief tomorrow," Gavin said, sitting on the log across from him. "I'm going to tell Rahimi the portage plan is set back a day." He stopped, looked at the fire. "I felt stranded out there. When the bag went under, I had six people and no idea where we were, and that scared me more than the water did." Ali kept turning the stick. Then he said, quietly, "I lost the heron. Two weeks of coming out here at dawn." Gavin hadn't prepared for that, and for a moment the old sentence, you did it to yourself, rose in him like a bubble in still water. He let it pass. "The heron's probably still here," he said. "They don't go far. Kelly-Anne saw one this morning past the second point."

In the morning Gavin gave the report to Mr. Rahimi in exactly the shape he'd practised, and then went further, proposing that the group take an hour before departure to circle back to the second point so Ali could try again, on the condition that the camera stayed in the dry bag until they were beached. It was a nascent plan, half-formed, and he said so; Rahimi looked at him for a long moment and wrote something in the margin of his clipboard. That afternoon Gavin sat in the bow while Ali filmed from the stable rock at the water's edge, and after twenty minutes of nothing but wind, the heron came around the point low and slow, feet trailing like a second pair of wings.

"Tell me you got it," Gavin called.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
The barn behind Grandmother's house had been a summer theatre once, before Ethan was born, and the stage was still there, a plywood platform with a faded square of carpet nailed to it. Ethan had claimed it for his one-act, the directing project Mr. Barrett had approved for the spring festival on the condition that Ethan "show some authority," words that had followed him home like a wasp.

Authority, in practice, meant asking his two friends to move a sofa. Tiago carried one end, Rosalie the other, and they set it down stage left, where Ethan wanted it. By the second scene it had migrated a full pace toward centre. By the third it sat almost in the wings, as though it were shy, or as though Tiago kept nudging it with his knee during his big monologue about leaving town.

"It walks," Rosalie said, hands on her hips. "You've directed a haunted sofa."

Ethan crouched and studied the plywood. His grandfather, when he still ran the barn shows, had kept a toolbox under the stage, and Ethan had found it that first week: hinges, a stub of chalk, and several fat rolls of coloured tape, neon pink and acid yellow, still tacky at the edges. He peeled a length of pink from the roll, tore it with his teeth, and laid a short strip at each sofa leg, then a second strip where the sofa actually belonged. The strips looked like small bright wounds on the grey wood.

"What's that called?" Tiago asked, squishing the tape with his sneaker.

"Spike tape," Ethan said. "It marks where furniture and actors go on the stage floor."

Tiago nodded slowly, the way he did when he was deciding whether a thing was cool or embarrassing, and then knelt to add a yellow spike for his own starting position, carefully, like a man planting a flag. That was the trouble with Tiago, Ethan thought: he would lionize the smallest job if you let him, turn a strip of tape into a ceremony, and it was hard to tell whether that helped the play or merely made everything slower and stranger and, somehow, better.

Rosalie wanted more. She had said so, once, quietly, while Tiago was outside on his phone: her character had four lines and a death that happened offstage, and she had been rehearsing the death in the mirror, she admitted, the walk offstage, the pause before it. She wanted the walk to mean something. Ethan had been directing her like furniture, he realized, blocking her from door to sofa and back, and so he gave her a spike of her own, a yellow mark downstage right, and told her the death could start there, that she could take all the time in the world crossing to the wings.

The real argument came on Friday. Tiago wanted his monologue downstage centre, three steps forward, big and loud, the barn doors open behind him like a church. Ethan kept pulling him back toward the sofa, toward the pink spikes, because the whole design of the play, as he'd drawn it in his notebook, was about people trapped in one room, and a boy marching to the edge of the stage telling the audience he was leaving was a lie the play couldn't afford. They stood on opposite ends of the plywood, and Tiago said, "You're directing like a traffic cop," and Ethan said, "You're acting like this is your play," and Rosalie, who had been stretching on the haunted sofa, said, "Gentlemen, the dead girl has an idea."

Her idea was a compromise, though compromise felt too small a word for what it did. Tiago could take his three steps forward, but not to centre; he'd stop on his own yellow spike, just past the sofa, close enough that the room still held him, and he'd say the speech not to the audience but to Rosalie, who would be sitting on the sofa pretending not to listen. The speech became an accusation. The room won and Tiago won at the same time, a little détente negotiated by a girl with four lines, and Ethan taped a new mark where Tiago's feet landed so he could find it again in the dark.

Rehearsals still had their disasters. The mosquitos were endemic to the barn by June, and Rosalie swatted one off her script and said her death scene now had sound design. The sofa, spikes or no spikes, still trembled when Tiago slammed his hand on its arm, and once skidded half an inch, and Ethan caught Tiago's eye across the stage and they both let it go, because half an inch was within tolerance. Ethan learned things Mr. Barrett had never said aloud: that actors find their own reasons if you give them a mark to stand on, that some nights you hold the shape of the play and some nights you let it bend, and that he could not always tell which night was which.

On the last rehearsal before the festival, Grandmother came out with a plate of sliced peaches and sat in the front row of folding chairs, the only audience they'd had. Tiago hit his mark without looking. Rosalie began her long walk to the wings, unhurried, her hand trailing along the sofa back, and the barn went quiet enough that Ethan could hear the tape sticking softly to her shoe as she crossed the pink line and stepped into the dark.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
Laurence had planned to spend Saturday at Delaney's, but her mother's sitter cancelled and the rule was absolute: no empty house until the probation of last March wore off. So she sat in the corner of her mother's office with her backpack as a footrest, watching rain snake down the window and listening to the radiator tick. On the desk beside her, her mother's screensaver shifted from quarterly charts to a photo of the two of them at the lake, then back, as if the company could not decide which version of them it preferred.

At 2:41 her phone buzzed. Delaney had dropped a photograph into the group chat: a street turned to brown water, a car submerged to its windows, someone's front door open like a mouth. Below it she'd written, "This is Millbrook RIGHT NOW. The dam's failing. Council meeting is at seven and they're going to pretend it's fine. Everyone share this before five so they can't ignore it."

Steven replied with three exclamation points and a repost, already made, ready to send. Laurence looked at the photo for a long moment. Her mother typed on, amortizing some client's loan across fifteen years of spreadsheets, entirely unaware that Millbrook, twenty minutes east, was supposedly drowning.

Something about the image bothered her, though she could not have said what at first. Then it came to her: the light. It was the flat white light of an overcast morning, and today's rain had come in sideways and gold at the edges. She scrolled back through her camera roll to a screenshot from March and compared skies like a detective matching fingerprints.

She typed "search by image" into the search bar, half expecting the idea to be impossible. But the first result was a help page explaining that Google had added search by image in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web. She copied the link to Delaney's photo, pasted it into the little camera icon, and hit enter, her heartbeat ridiculous for what was, technically, a box on a screen.

The results loaded. A weather blog from 2016. A news article about flooding in a town in Ohio, dated 2014. An insurance company's disaster page. Same car, same open door, same brown water. Not Millbrook. Not now. Not even this decade. She checked twice, then a third time, opening the oldest result, and in every one the photograph wore a different caption like a coat someone else had lent it.

"It's from 2014," she typed into the chat. "Somebody's recycling it." Steven answered with a sullen "so what, dams still fail," and Delaney's reply came fast: "You don't know that's not Millbrook too. It could have happened both places. I'm posting at five either way." Laurence sat back. Delaney wasn't lying, exactly; she was certain, which was different and worse, because certainty recruits people who would never tell a lie on purpose. Laurence remembered her grandmother forwarding a similar photo last spring, a shark on a highway, and how the whole family had believed it until someone checked. She had laughed then. It was less funny from the inside.

She thought of Mr. Holloway, who taught civics and ran the debate club, and his endless word "dialectic," the way he pushed them to hold two claims at once and let them argue it out. She held them now: the dam might genuinely be a problem; the photo was genuinely fake. Both could be true. The trick was that only one of them was hers to prove, and she had proved it, and the other one, the question of whether the dam needed fixing, stayed exactly as uncertain as it had been at 2:41. That was the part Delaney would not want to hear, that being right about the photo made her right about nothing else.

She called her mother over, held the phone up, and walked her through it: the pasted link, the camera icon, the 2014 news article with its matching picture. Her mother looked at the screen, then at her, with an expression Laurence filed away for later. "Text Delaney's mom," her mother said quietly, and turned back to her spreadsheets, but slower, as if the numbers had lost some of their authority.

At 4:52 Delaney posted something else entirely: the county's actual dam inspection report, public record, dated last month, with a paragraph about delayed repairs. Underneath she'd written, "This one's real. Checked it myself." Steven replied, "how," and Laurence watched the typing bubble appear and disappear twice before Delaney answered with the camera emoji and a link to the help page. Laurence smiled at the rain-gold window, screensaver ticking quietly toward the lake, and screenshotted the whole thread.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
Mya set the cutting board across the kitchen table like a drawing board and weighted the corners with mugs from the dish rack. The collage for her portfolio submission was due in three days, and the photograph she wanted at its center, a shot of the river flats behind her aunt's house, refused to behave. She had cut it twice already, and both times the horizon sat dead in the middle of the composition like a fence nobody wanted.

Her mother passed through to the stove, looked over her shoulder, and said nothing, which in their house was a kind of permission. Mya trimmed a strip of newsprint the blue-gray of storm light and slid it along the bottom edge, testing. The kettle ticked as it cooled. Outside, a neighbor's car door closed twice, the second slam softer, an argument finishing itself.

Audrina arrived at four with Kennedy, both of them still in their work shirts from the community art studio where they volunteered on Saturdays, Kennedy's smock rolled under one arm like a drowned flag. They had claimed the kitchen table months ago as project territory, and Mya cleared the mugs to make room while Kennedy unfolded the smock and shook crumbs off it.

"Same river picture?" Audrina asked, hanging her jacket on the chair back.

"It keeps looking like a postcard," Mya said. "The kind they sell at gas stations."

Kennedy leaned over the photo, chin propped on her fist. "At the studio Saturday, this kid, maybe fourteen, was painting a lake, and I told him to put the horizon a third of the way down. He asked me who made that rule."

"What did you say?"

"I said it's the rule of thirds. And then I looked it up on the office computer because honestly I didn't know. The phrase was first written down by John Thomas Smith, in his 1797 book, Remarks on Rural Scenery." Kennedy said it carefully, the way she recited supply orders. "A guy writing about rural scenery, two hundred years ago, and we're still handing it to teenagers like it's physics."

Mya turned the photograph ninety degrees and looked at it sideways, the horizon now a vertical seam. "So Smith just made it up? One man, one opinion?"

"More or less. He noticed painters did it and gave it a name."

"That's either depressing or emancipating," Mya said. "I can't decide which." She meant it as a joke but it came out flat, and Audrina laughed anyway, the laugh doing the work the words hadn't.

She cut the photograph again, this time along the line of the far bank, and pushed the sky upward until the horizon fell a third of the way from the top. The flats opened below it, all that gray water suddenly consequential, and Kennedy said, "There, see," and Mya almost said yes. Instead she sat back and felt the small dishonesty of it. The version was better. It was also a version a hundred thousand people had made before her, and better in exactly the way they had all been better.

She thought of pre-calculus, junior year, the way Ms. Bighorn had once stopped a lesson on limits to say that an asymptote was a line a curve approaches but never touches, and that some things were like that on purpose. At the time Mya had thought it was a throwaway remark, teacherly poetry. Now she moved the horizon a fraction below the third and watched the composition get worse, moved it back, and understood that the rule was not a law but a curve she kept approaching. Smith had written down where the curve tended, not where it had to land. That was different. That was maybe everything.

"Who moved my smock," Kennedy said, not a question, digging under a fold of blue-gray paper.

"You put it on my side," Audrina said.

"That is not a thing. There are no sides of a kitchen table." The argument went on, mild and vitriolic at once, the way only old friends could manage, and Mya let it run behind her like radio. She took a second copy of the photograph from her folder, the one she'd printed as a spare, and began cutting it differently: horizon low, almost crushed under the sky, the water reduced to a bright ribbon. Wrong, probably. She pinned it to the corkboard by the fridge beside the obedient one and stood at the sink comparing them.

Her mother came through again with the laundry basket and paused at the corkboard long enough for Mya to notice her noticing. "That one," her mother said, and touched the crushed horizon, and kept walking toward the stairs.

"Your mom has terrible taste," Audrina said.

"She has taste from before the rule existed," Mya said, and heard how it wasn't quite a joke either. 1797 was not that long ago; people had balanced skies and water for centuries before Smith gave them a sentence to obey, and would go on doing it after the sentence wore out.

The kettle had gone cold. Mya sat back down at the table, took the pinned photograph down, and held the two versions side by side over the newsprint, one in each hand, the third-of-the-way horizon and the crushed one, the submission deadline on Friday and no sign yet of which picture was hers.

"Hand me the glue," she said.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Electricity is billed by the kilowatt-hour, so using 600 kilowatt-hours at 15 cents each costs 90 dollars, before any fixed monthly charges.
story:
The printouts sat on his grandfather's kitchen table, two apartment leases side by side, and Nathan had been staring at them long enough that the words had started to dissolve into texture. The first place, a one-bedroom above a bakery, charged seven hundred and eighty a month plus electric. The second, farther out past the bus depot, was seven hundred and twenty, heat included, but electricity on top of that, plus a forty-dollar parking fee his mother would laugh at and pay anyway. He was supposed to choose before orientation. He was seventeen, and the whole thing felt seismic, like a decision that would set the shape of everything after it, though he suspected that was the kind of thing people told themselves about decisions that were mostly about money.

"Nobody actually reads these," said Malcolm, who had come over with Mohamed-Amine because the grandfather's house had the good air conditioning and the grandmother's lemon cake. Malcolm leaned across the table, poking at the first lease with one finger. "You just pick the one with the nicer photos."

Mohamed-Aamine pulled out the chair opposite Nathan and sat down properly, the way he did everything, as if chairs were interviews. "My cousin got destroyed by a bill once. He thought heat was included. It was included until November."

"Then he should have read the lease," Nathan said, and immediately regretted the tone, because that was the whole problem, he had read them, twice, and they didn't say the thing he needed to know. "Neither of these says what the electric actually costs. It just says tenant pays electric. That could be anything."

The grandfather came in with three glasses of iced tea and set them down without asking whether anyone wanted tea, which was his way of saying sit still. He looked at the papers, then at Nathan, then went back to the den, and Nathan heard the television resume its low murmur, some baseball game the grandfather was only half prognosticating about, calling plays before they happened and being wrong at a rate he seemed to enjoy.

Mohamed-Amine turned the second lease around to face himself and read in silence for a while. "You could just ask them," he said finally. "The landlord. What the person before you paid."

"Would they know that?"

Mohamed-Amine shrugged. "The bill goes to the address. They see it, or they file it. My uncle manages four buildings and he knows every tenant's usage. He says people lie about how much they'll use and the meter doesn't."

Nathan found the number for the second apartment's landlord in the listing, and after a false start and a hold message that looped a saxophone riff until it became the leitmotif of his entire afternoon, a woman answered. He asked, feeling awkward, whether she could tell him the previous tenant's typical electricity usage, and she said, sure, it ran about six hundred kilowatt-hours a month. He asked what a kilowatt-hour cost around there and she said fifteen cents, roughly, depending on the month. He wrote both numbers on the margin of the lease while Malcolm mouthed "kilowatt-hour" at Mohamed-Amine in a fake posh accent, which Nathan ignored.

He did the math out loud, mostly to keep Malcolm from doing it wrong. Six hundred kilowatt-hours at fifteen cents each was ninety dollars, and that was before whatever fixed monthly charges the utility added on, which the landlord said she couldn't speak to. So the farther apartment wasn't really seven hundred and twenty. It was seven hundred and twenty plus ninety plus forty for parking, and the fixed charges on top of that, still unknown, while the bakery apartment was seven hundred and eighty plus electric, and he had no usage figure for it at all because he hadn't thought to ask, and the landlord there hadn't picked up the second time he called.

"So the far one is at least eight fifty," Mohamed-Amine said, "and probably more, and you still don't know the bakery one."

"And I don't know if I'd use six hundred," Nathan said. "The guy before me might have run a space heater all winter. Or mined bitcoin. I'd have my laptop and a lamp."

The grandfather appeared again, tea refills nobody had finished, and stood reading the numbers upside down with his hands on his hips. "You know what you don't like yet," he said. "That's not the same as knowing what you like." Then he went back to the den, and the crowd on the television made a sound like something had gone over a wall.

Nathan looked at the two pages, the margins now crowded with his arithmetic, the ninety written and circled and added and circled again. He picked up his phone and dialed the bakery landlord one more time, and while it rang he pulled the first lease toward him and, in the empty space beside the rent clause, wrote the question he would ask if anyone ever answered: previous tenant, typical usage, please.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void.
story:
Aidan had the laptop open on the kitchen table by eight, the house still smelling of his mother's coffee though she had left for work an hour before. On the screen was a class called Student with three private fields, name, idNumber, and gpa, and beneath it a test that was supposed to create a Student and print the values back. The printed values were null, zero, and zero. He ran it again and got the same thing, as if the machine were correcting him out of some congenital stubbornness rather than following instructions.

He had written the class the way he always wrote methods, starting with public, then void, then the name. That felt right. Everything else in Java declared what it returned, so why should this be different? He read his own code the way you reread a text message you already sent, looking for the exact place it went wrong and not finding it.

He texted Kyra, who had finished the assignment two days earlier. "did your student object print the fields right away or did you have to do something." She typed back slowly, the three dots appearing and vanishing, a mannerism he had come to read as her thinking out loud on the other end. "mine worked first try. why, what's yours doing." He sent her a photo of the output, the null sitting in the middle of the line like a hole in the sentence.

"send the class," she wrote, and he did, and then nothing for four minutes. When her reply came it was one line: "look at your constructor." He scrolled up to his own code and looked. He read the word constructor and understood, dimly, that this was what the method was called, though he could not have said what made it one.

He opened a message to Mr. Bekele, because it was due at midnight and he did not want to spend the evening guessing. "Mr. Bekele, my Student object comes back with null fields even though I set them in the method with the same name as the class. I attached the file. Is my test wrong?" He hit send before he could edit it into something less admitting.

While he waited he tried the one difference he could see between his code and Kyra's, which he did not let himself look at directly, since that would be copying. Hers was shorter at the top of that method. He put his cursor at the start of the line, selected the word void, and deleted it. Nothing else changed. The line now read public Student, which looked wrong to him, like a sentence answering itself.

He ran the test. The output printed a name, an ID, a GPA. He sat back and looked at it for a while, then wrote the fact into his notebook in the margin where he kept things he did not trust himself to remember: a constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void. Saying it to himself that way, as a rule with edges, made it feel less like luck.

Mr. Bekele's reply arrived at 9:40, and it was not what Aidan expected. "Your test is fine. I did not fix your file. Look at the version history." Aidan opened it and scrolled back through the saves. There were two entries from 6:12 and 6:15 that evening, before his message. At 6:12 the file had void in front of Student. At 6:15 it did not. Someone had edited the file while he was in the kitchen making toast.

He texted Patrick. "were you on my repo." The reply came fast, too fast for innocence: "you left it shared from the lab. i had the same bug. i fixed yours so i'd know the fix worked before i trusted it on mine." Aidan read it twice. So the run that had worked, the run he had credited to his own deletion, had been Patrick's deletion already sitting in the file. He had not selected void and removed it; he had selected void and removed it a second time, over an absence.

He thought about writing back that it wasn't cool to change someone's code, and he thought about writing thanks, and both felt like claims he could not fully support. The fact in his notebook was still true; that much he had verified himself, deleting and retyping void four more times and watching the nulls return and vanish like a tide. What he could not verify was which of them, in the small dark of that evening, had actually taught him.

The test passed again. He committed the file, left the sharing on, and pushed.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: A Pareto improvement, named after economist Vilfredo Pareto, is a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off.
story:
Alicia set her fork down before her mother finished asking. "Troy needs the car Thursday nights for his shift, and I need it Saturday mornings for the lab job. That's all. I already worked it out."

"Worked it out," her father repeated, not looking up from his plate.

"Mr. Oliveira mentioned it in econ, this thing called a Pareto improvement. It's named after an economist, Vilfredo Pareto. It means a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off." She pushed the rice around her plate. "Right now nobody has the car Thursday night, because you and Mom use it. If I drive Troy, he's better off, and nobody's worse off. It's a Pareto improvement. It's like the one thing in the whole class that actually made sense."

The kitchen went quiet except for the fan over the stove. Keely had texted Alicia twice that afternoon about Saturday, and the phone sat face-down beside Alicia's water glass like a second plate she was avoiding.

"Who pays for the gas," her father said.

"Split it. I did the math."

"And if he scratches it?"

"Then it's on him. I wrote it down." She pulled the folded page from under her thigh and flattened it beside the salt. Four lines. Thursday, Saturday, gas split, damage on the driver. Her mother read it without touching it, the way people read bills.

"You've thought about this more than you thought about your college essay," her mother said, and laughed, but the laugh had a wire in it.

Here was the part Alicia hadn't put on the page. Keely's Saturdays. Keely's mother worked Saturdays, and Keely took her little brother to swim practice at nine, which was the same hour Alicia needed the car for the lab, and for two months Alicia had been the one driving all three of them, looping across town, arriving at the lab eleven minutes late every single time. If Alicia took the car alone on Saturdays, Keely's brother missed swim. He was eight. He'd cried about it once, in the driveway, which was unbearable in a way Alicia couldn't name.

"Saturday's complicated," her mother said, watching her face.

"It's fine."

"Is Keely fine?"

"She's fine." The word came out noncommittal, half-swallowed, and everyone at the table heard it land wrong.

Her father put his fork across his plate like a punctuation mark. "You know what I keep hearing? A lot about who's better off, and nothing about who's worse off if you're wrong. That's the part people skip."

"I didn't skip it. That's the whole point of the rule. Nobody's worse off."

"The rule's on paper, Alicia. People aren't."

She stared at the page, mesmerized for a second by her own handwriting, so neat, so complete, covering exactly as much as it covered. Thursday: Troy better off, parents no worse off, since they didn't use the car then anyway. Saturday: Alicia better off. And Keely, and an eight-year-old with goggles, somewhere off the edge of the page where the math stopped.

"I could do Saturdays every other week," she said slowly. "Alternating with Keely, but then her brother still misses half his practices, and I'm still late half the time, so it's just spreading the loss around instead of eliminating it. That's not the same thing." She heard her own voice change pitch, the way it did when she was actually thinking instead of performing. "Maybe there is no version where nobody's worse off. Maybe the rule only tells you when to keep looking, not when to stop."

Her mother tilted her head. "So what are you going to do?"

"I don't know yet. Troy's shift ends at ten. The bus runs till eleven. If he takes the bus Thursday, I don't need to drive him at all, and Thursday stops mattering." She was already reaching for the phone, flipping it over, thumbs moving. To Keely: if I can only do half the Saturdays, would your brother's practice move to the Y? Their pool does Sundays. She set it down again, face-up this time.

"That's the first honest thing you've said all dinner," her father said, and picked his fork back up.

The phone buzzed against the wood. Keely: checking with mom. might work?? Alicia picked up her plate and carried it to the sink, and stood there with the water running over her hands, watching the leftover rice spiral down the drain.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
The hamburgers came off the grill at noon, and by four o'clock they were still sitting in their foil pan on the porch rail of his grandfather's house, and Joseph was the only one who seemed to notice. The rest of the family had drifted to the back garden, where his uncle was teaching Joaquin and Shane a card game involving a great deal of shouting. Joseph stood at the screen door with a roll of plastic bags in his hand, counting backward through the afternoon.

He had texted Mr. Mensah an hour ago, hoping for a straight answer, but his old biology teacher only replied with a link. Joseph read it standing in the kitchen with the phone balanced on the counter between a bowl of potato salad and his grandmother's dented meat thermometer. Perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when the temperature was above 90. He read it twice. The thermometer, when he jabbed the nearest burger, read 91 in the meat and 88 in the air beside the pan, which meant the one-hour rule was the one that had already been broken, twice over.

His grandmother came in for more ice and saw him bagging the chicken. "Leave that, sweetheart, I'll do it. We never waste anything in this house." She reached past him and pulled the pan back toward the counter. She had grown up with seven siblings and an unspoken injunction against throwing away food, and Joseph knew that arguing with it directly would get him nowhere.

"Grandma, it sat out all afternoon."

"So it sat out. It smells fine." She lifted a wing to her nose and inhaled, a gesture that instantiated her entire position better than any argument could: the senses, she believed, were the original food safety system.

Joaquin appeared in the doorway with cards still in his hand. "Your uncle wants to know if there's more pie, and also Shane says you abandoned us."

"There's pie," Joseph said. "There might not be chicken." He showed them the thermometer, then the number on his phone. He didn't explain it. He let the two things sit next to each other the way evidence sits next to a crime, and Joaquin, who wanted very much to be a lawyer someday and had spent the entire drive up arguing that rules only mattered when someone enforced them, studied the screen with genuine interest.

"That's the whole game right there," Joaquin said. "Two hours under 140. One hour if it's over 90 outside." He tapped the screen. "It's basically a rule about the window closing faster on a hot day. Like in sports."

"Except nobody blew a whistle," Shane said from behind him, mouth full of pie. "It's still sitting there looking fine. I'd eat it."

"You would eat a tire if it had barbecue sauce on it," Joaquin said.

His grandfather came in last, drawn by the gathering, and stood a moment watching them hover over the meat thermometer like it was a museum piece. He was a quiet man who had spent forty years breeding peppers in the side garden, and he listened to Joseph lay it out without interrupting: the hours, the temperature, the porch rail in full sun. When Joseph finished, his grandfather picked up one of the chicken wings his wife had set aside, turned it over once, and set it down again.

"You know," he said, "the peppers I grow, two plants from the same seed packet can look nothing alike. Different heights, different fruit. That's phenotypic variation, what the environment does to the same genes." He nodded toward the porch. "Food's the same, I suppose. Two pans sitting out. One in the shade, one in the sun. Not the same chicken anymore, even if it started that way."

"You're saying throw it out?" his grandmother said sharply.

"I'm saying the boy did the arithmetic. That's more than any of us did."

Joseph stood with the bag half-tied in his fist. He was certain about the chicken in the sun, and uncertain about the potato salad, which had gone into the refrigerator and out again twice for serving and whose clock he could not honestly reconstruct. That part he would have to guess at, and he hated guessing in front of Joaquin, who kept score. He wrote a line on the masking tape label, not certain, and put it on the middle shelf where the morning light would catch it.

His grandmother carried the foil pan to the compost herself, walking fast so no one would see her face, and came back wiping her hands on her apron. "Next year," she said, "you're in charge of the leftovers from the start. You and your thermometer."

"Deal," Joseph said, and went back out to the porch to watch the last of the sun go down over the pepper garden.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: The transition, or bridge, is the passage in the exposition that modulates from the home key to the second key, and it often uses busier, less tuneful material.
story:
The community centre kept its piano in a room that smelled of chlorine from the pool next door, and Charlie had claimed it every Tuesday since September because Ms. Sutton's theory class had overflowed the library. She spread the score of Mozart's K. 333 across the music stand and set her pencil down beside it like a surgical instrument. The assignment was due Thursday: mark the exposition, the development, the recapitulation, and she had been circling the same sixteen bars for forty minutes.

"Found the second theme yet?" Brooklyn leaned in the doorway with a sandwich, though eating was technically banned, which Brooklyn treated as an incentive.

"I found a second theme. I don't know if it's the one." Charlie played the passage, then the one before it, then frowned at her own pencil marks, which had multiplied until the page looked annotated by a distracted bird.

Anaelle arrived carrying two highlighters, pink and green, and the conviction that colour-coding solved everything. She sat on the bench's far end and read over Charlie's shoulder. "You've got the first theme ending at bar ten."

"That's what I thought. But then Ms. Sutton said the first theme is tuneful, and this bit at bar eleven is still tuneful, so where does it stop?" Charlie played bars eleven through twenty. The melody thinned out, the left hand started churning, and the tune dissolved into something busier, arrows and runs, music that seemed to be going somewhere rather than being somewhere.

"Ugh," said Brooklyn, around the sandwich. "It's like the music dried out."

"It desiccated," Anaelle said, pleased with herself. "Very technical."

Charlie played it again. Something changed under her fingers partway through, a slippage, and she stopped with her hand flat on the keys. "It's not just busier. Listen." She played the two passages back to back, then hummed the second one, then humed it lower. "It's not in the same key anymore. Somewhere in there it modulates."

"Modulates," Brooklyn repeated, in the tone of someone who suspected the word of being an excuse.

"Changes key. From the home key to the second key." Charlie drew a bracket with her pencil. "So this busy part isn't a theme at all. It's the thing that gets you from the first key to the second one."

"That's the transition," Anaelle said, paging through her notes. "Or the bridge. It's in my homework, look, it says the transition is the passage in the exposition that modulates from the home key to the second key, and it often uses busier, less tunely material."

"Less tuneful."

"That's what I said."

"You said tunely. Like a cartoon character." But Charlie was already writing in the margin, and her hand was steadier than it had been all afternoon. The problem that had seemed tautological an hour ago, you know the first theme ends where the transition begins, and the transition begins where the first theme ends, had cracked open, because the passage itself had a signature. Busy, unlovely, purposeful. She found the second key on the keyboard, confirmed it against the score, and drew a line straight down the page. First theme. Bridge. Second theme, tuneful again in the new key, like the music had crossed a river and wrung itself out.

"You look smug," Brooklyn observed.

"I look like a savant. A very slow one." Charlie marked the exposition's end with a double bar of her own devising, then kept going into the development, where Mozart took her themes apart and let them wander through keys with no home in sight, and she understood why that section felt restless in her hands even before she could name it.

At the door, Brooklyn paused. "So Thursday you just hand in this page with the pink and green?"

"The pink and green were my idea," Anaelle said.

"The pink and green were load-bearing," Charlie said, and capped her pencil.

She stayed after they left. She still couldn't decide whether the recapitulation began exactly where she'd put it or two bars later, and she played the spot four times, letting the repeat of the opening theme argue with her pencil line. The room had gone quiet enough that she could hear the pool clock through the wall, ticking off the beats she couldn't find in the score. She left both possibilities marked, one in pencil, one faintly in pink, turned off the piano lamp, and carried the page out under her arm like something that might still change its mind.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
The bleachers at the community field were old enough that the paint had gone chalky, and Savannah chose the third row because it put the sun behind her. Her father spread a blanket over two seats for her grandmother, who did not need a blanket but accepted it anyway. On the field below, the county select team was warming up for the semifinal, and Treyton's younger brother was starting at left wing, which was the reason eleven of them had given up a Saturday.

Savannah had brought her referee certification handbook in her bag, folded open to the section she kept rereading. She had passed the online test three weeks ago, and Mr. Wu, who ran the youth league and lived two streets over, had said he would assign her lines next weekend if she was serious. She was serious, though she could not have said exactly why. Something about knowing the rules well enough to make a call in front of a hundred people who were certain she was wrong.

Daniella arrived late, holding a soda and a folded piece of paper. "Treyton wrote you something," she said. "He had to leave for his shift."

The note was in Treyton's bad handwriting, the kind that leaned backward. Savannah, the paper said, I know you're studying the offside law like it's a final. Two things I bet you five dollars each nobody at that game knows. One, you can stand in an offside position all day and it's nothing by itself. You only get penalized when you get involved in active play. Two, there is no offside from a throw-in, a goal kick, or a corner. Watch somebody yell about it today and collect your money. He had signed it with a small drawing of a linesman's flag.

She folded the note along its creases and put it in her pocket. The first half was physical and low-scoring, 1-0 off a long shot that the goalkeeper touched but could not hold. In the row behind them, her uncle criticized every decision the assistant referee made, loudly enough that the grandmother told him twice to lower his voice. Savannah followed the offside line herself out of habit, tracking the second-to-last defender, and once she disagreed with a flag that went up. She kept that to herself.

The equalizer came in the sixtieth minute, from a corner. The ball curved toward the near post, a tangle of players rose for it, and the winger headed it in from what looked, to half the stands, like an illegal position. Her uncle was on his feet before the ball finished bouncing in the net. "Offside! He was three meters behind the line!" The word came out flattened and furious, the way people enunciate when they want a referee to hear them across a field.

"That's a corner," Savannah said. She had not planned to speak, but the note was in her pocket and the fact was in her head, and they lined up together. "You can't be offside from a corner. He could stand behind the whole team and it's nothing." Her uncle turned around fully, so she went on, slower. "Even the other way, standing offside isn't an offence by itself. It only gets penalized when he's involved in active play." Somebody's father two rows down said she was wrong. Daniella said, "She has the badge, actually."

The goal stood. The referee pointed to the center circle, the assistant's flag stayed down, and play resumed while her uncle muttered into his jacket. Savannah felt something in her settle, and something else stay restless. She had been right, and being right had felt less like triumph and more like standing on a spot she could not see the edges of. She understood the words she had said. She was less sure she could apply them at full speed, in real time, with a crowd behind her and Mr. Wu watching from the touchline, where he now stood in his league windbreaker, talking to the fourth official. Whether she could carry a law cleanly from a page into her own consciousness, and out through a flag at the right instant, was a question the bleachers could not answer.

After the final whistle, 2-1, she walked down past the concession stand to where Mr. Wu was collecting the corner flags. He looked up and asked whether she had enjoyed the match. She said she had, mostly, and then asked, as evenly as she could, what time he wanted her there next Saturday.

He said nine sharp, and handed her the first flag.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
story:
Rhys arrived eleven minutes after four, dropping his bag onto the library table where Maelle had already spread out her debate binder, and before he even sat down he said it again. "If I'd left five minutes earlier, I'd have caught the bus. Then I wouldn't have been late to practice, and Coach wouldn't have benched me for Saturday."

"You said that at lunch," Royce said, not looking up from his laptop. "Twice."

"Because it's true."

"It's true that you missed the bus," Royce said. "The rest of it, you can't know. You can never check it."

Maelle slid a highlighted article across the table, mostly to change the subject, because they had a resolution to prepare for and the tournament was in six days. The school board was considering moving start times an hour later, and Maelle was assigned to argue for it, which she had privately begun to regret. The research was a mess of competing studies, and Rhys's sulking wasn't helping. "Can we codify our points? Claim, evidence, response. We need structure or we'll get destroyed on cross."

Rhys ignored the binder. "How can you say I can't know? Five minutes. The bus runs on a schedule."

Royce turned his laptop around. On the screen was a philosophy page he'd apparently been reading all afternoon, because beneath it sat three more tabs about conditionals. "This kind of sentence has a name," he said. "A counterfactual conditional. If Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it."

"She doesn't own a donkey," Maelle said.

"Exactly. That's part of it. It describes what would have been true if things had been different, and usually the if part is false. Sally doesn't own a donkey. You didn't leave five minutes earlier. There's no world where you can go look."

Rhys leaned back in his chair with the patience of someone humouring a younger sibling. "So what's the point of ever saying it?"

Maelle had been half-listening, half-reading her own evidence, but something in the question pulled at her. She'd spent two days assembling studies about sleep and attendance, all of them describing what would happen if the board changed the times, and none of it checkable, not really, not until after the decision. She wrote in the margin of her binder, in small letters, then crossed it out, then wrote it again. "It's not useless," she said slowly. "You use it to plan. Before the fact, you can still choose. The bus is tomorrow too."

"Tomorrow's a different conditional," Royce said. "Not counterfactual. You can still leave five minutes earlier tomorrow."

"Then I will," Rhys said, with a doctrinaire firmness that suggested he thought the whole conversation had been arranged to insult him. "And I'll catch it, and that will prove I was right today."

"It'll prove nothing about today," Royce said.

From the front desk, Mr. Paquette, the librarian, who had been reshelving returns near their table and clearly listening longer than any of them had noticed, cleared his throat. "You three might want the Garner book," he said. "It has a whole chapter on conditionals, better than that website. But I'll tell you one thing for free." He held up a volume bound in grey cloth. "The bus on Route Nine has had a GPS tracker since September. The school posts the logs online. Anyone could check when it actually came."

There was a silence in which Maelle watched Rhys's face do something complicated. He took out his phone. His thumb moved. The screen lit his chin from below, and his shoulders dropped.

"That's not the time I thought," he said quietly.

"Which way?" Royce asked.

"Later. It came later. If I'd left on time, I'd have missed it anyway." He set the phone face down on the table as though it had lied to him personally.

Maelle laughed before she could stop herself, and then stopped herself, because Rhys looked genuinely wounded, and also because a thought had begun assembling in her head that she didn't like. The counterfactual he'd been reciting all day, the one Royce had called untestable, had turned out to be testable after all, just not in the direction anyone expected. If he had left five minutes earlier, he would still have been benched. The sentence was false in a way none of them could have guessed, and it had taken a stranger's perspicacity and a county transit website to show it.

Then the rest of it arrived. She turned to her binder, flipped back two pages to her notes from Monday, and found what she had been trying not to find: the debate outline Royce had photographed for her, the one Rhys had run across town to deliver when she left it in the gym, the errand that had made him miss his usual bus in the first place.

"Rhys," she said. "You were late Monday. Getting my notes."

"So?"

"So the conditional cuts both ways." She closed the binder. "If I hadn't left my outline behind, you'd have caught your regular bus, and Coach never would have benched you."

Rhys looked at her for a long moment. Down at his phone. Over at the grey book in Mr. Paquette's hand, still extended, unclaimed.

"Then argue for the later start time," he said. "Because if school starts an hour later, I can sleep in, and I never have to do you any favours again."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so customers with no orders disappear from its results entirely.
story:
Thomas had assumed his mother's office would be quiet on a Saturday, but the third floor hummed, and a woman from analytics named Ms. Addo had left a note on the desk he was borrowing: "If you touch the sample database, don't touch the real one." He was there because his mother worked Saturdays in August and had refused, with a certain belligerent patience, to leave him home alone with a broken air conditioner. He spread his notebook beside the keyboard and read the assignment from Ms. Addo's summer packet again, though he had already read it four times on the train.

The task was to find every customer who had never placed an order. The office kept two tables for practicing, CUSTOMERS and ORDERS, and Ms. Addo had promised that the answer was not zero. "The quiet ones matter," she had written at the bottom of the page, underlined once. Thomas did not know what she meant by that yet, and did not particularly care; he cared about the fact that Mattea, who sat beside him in class and had finished the packet in July, kept texting him about it.

Mattea wanted the office's real numbers. She had heard from her cousin, who worked in memberships at a gym, that lapsed members who got a phone call in their first silent month came back at twice the usual rate, and she had decided, in the way she decided things, that the same logic applied to any business with a customer list. "Ask your mom's office for their inactive customers," she had texted that morning. "I want to see if the pattern holds before I do my essay on it." Thomas had said maybe. He was beginning to understand that maybe was a word that could transmute into yes if he let it sit long enough.

He wrote the query the way that seemed obvious. He joined the customers to the orders, because that was what he had in his notes from the spring, and asked for the rows where the order side was empty. The screen returned nothing. Not an error, not a warning, just a clean blank grid, as though the question itself had been politely deleted. He ran it again. Blank. He checked that the tables had rows in them, hundreds in one, dozens in the other, and felt the particular humiliation of a machine agreeing with him too quickly.

Elisha had told him once, in the library, something about joins, but Elisha explained things the way a person reads terms and conditions, fast and without believing anyone was listening. Thomas opened the practice workbook anyway and found the page. INNER JOIN, it said. He said it out loud to the empty cubicle, softly, like testing a word in a language he was supposed to have been studying. He wrote it into the query in place of what he had typed before, ran it once more, and understood, staring at the blank grid, that an INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables. The customers with no orders were not in the results because they had nothing to match. They had not been counted or flagged or filtered. They had disappeared from the results entirely, as if silence made a person invisible.

He sat back. Somewhere behind him a printer coughed out a page of something to do with jurisprudence, his mother's department, thick binders full of cases and precedents, and he thought, briefly and without wanting to, that the law and the database agreed on one point: what goes unrecorded does not exist. Then he began again, differently, listing all the customers and asking which ones were missing from the matched set, and this time the grid filled. Eleven names. Eleven customers with no orders, sitting quietly in a table all afternoon while his first query insisted they were not there.

He photographed the screen for Ms. Addo, then hesitated, because Mattea's essay wanted the office's real list, and the real list was not his to hand over, and he had said maybe partly because he had wanted her to keep texting him through August. He typed out a reply and deleted it twice before settling on a compromise he did not feel certain of: "The query works. Whether we can run it on their actual customers is a different question. I'll ask Monday." He sent it, then copied his corrected query into his notebook in slow capitals so the joins were unmistakable, INNER on one line, the missing ones on the next.

His mother appeared in the doorway with her coat already on, keys in hand, and asked if he had finished his homework in her office of all places. He told her eleven and pointed at the screen. She leaned over his shoulder, one hand on the back of the chair, and read the names slowly, the way she read everything, and said, "The Henderson account. I wondered what happened to them."

"Nothing happened to them," Thomas said. "That's the whole point."

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2000 study led by psychologist William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions.
story:
The pool at the community centre had gone turbid again, the lane ropes dissolving into green murk halfway down, so Ms. Carvalho moved practice to the dryland room and told everyone to bring their running shoes. Olivia had meant to use the bus ride to rehearse for her interview at Halloran's Bakery on Saturday, but she had fallen asleep against the window with her notes folded in her fist, and now the only preparation she had was a sugar-craving stomach and a pair of shaking hands.

"I'm going to fail," she told Andrei while they stretched against the wall.

"You say that before every time trial."

"And I'm usually right." She flexed her fingers, which had cramped around a pen the night before, filling out the section on strengths. Under it she had written, in smaller letters, none yet identified. She hadn't decided whether that was honesty or sabotage.

Andrei had his own problems. Ms. Carvalho had posted the relay roster on the door, and his name was in the second-fastest lane, which he considered a demotion, an insult, and possibly a clerical error, in that order. He spent the whole warm-up petitioning her with his eyes. She spent the whole warm-up not looking at him.

It was Imran who brought it up, during the water break, because Imran read everything and reported on it the way other people reported the weather. "My grandfather has me practise handshakes before interviews," he said, peeling an orange with his thumbnail. "He read about a study. A 2000 study led by a psychologist named William Chaplin. It found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favourable first impressions." He offered Olivia a segment, which she took, because being handed something and taking it felt like the first competent thing she'd done all week.

"Define firm," she said.

"Granny says dead fish helps no one. Also says bone-crusher helps no one. There is a middle country and you must live in it." Imran held out his hand, palm up, waiting.

They shook over the orange peels. His grip was steady, dry, brief. Hers, she could feel, was an apology. They tried again, and again, until Ms. Carvalho clapped her hands and called them back to the plyo boxes, and Olivia spent the lunges and the squat jumps thinking about the study, about how strange it was that a thing as arbitrary as a handshake could be measured at all, Chaplin and his colleagues in the year 2000 with their clipboards, counting favourableness like laps.

She tried to bring the two ideas together during the plank hold, which was a mistake, because thinking and planking do not mix. One idea was that a firm handshake was a performance, a trick, a costume you put on for a woman behind a bakery counter who would decide in ninety seconds whether you were trustworthy with the morning pastries. The other idea was that the performance changed you, that maybe if she gripped Imran's hand as though she meant it, some part of her would start to mean it, and the confidence would not be a lie so much as a rehearsal that eventually told the truth. She could not decide which idea she believed. She held the plank until her arms shook, and the uncertainty sat in her chest like a swallowed stone, and she thought, fine, let it stay. She did not have to settle it by Saturday.

After practice, Ms. Carvalho caught her at the door. "Halloran's still hiring?" she asked. Olivia had mentioned it once, weeks ago, in the middle of a set. "Tell her you can carry a fifty-pound flour sack. You can. I've watched you haul the equipment bin." She squeezed Olivia's shoulder once, briskly, and walked off toward the pump room, where Andrei was already waiting by the roster, pretending he had a question about the start times.

Olivia let herself out into the evening. The bus shelter smelled of wet leaves and someone's abandoned chips. She took out her notes, found the section on strengths, and drew a single line through none yet identified. Under it, after a moment, she wrote can carry fifty pounds of flour, and then, underneath that, small and neat, firm handshake, see: proof, Imran's grandfather. She held her right hand out in front of her, curled her fingers closed, and held the grip, in the empty shelter, for three full seconds.

"Middle country," she said to her own knuckles, and went to find the bus.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in his 1958 book The Uses of Argument, described an argument's backbone as a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant explaining why those grounds support the claim.
story:
