Mr. Lavoie's philosophy classroom smelled like dry-erase marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and on Tuesday mornings it belonged to a debate that had been running for three weeks: whether an artificial mind could deserve moral consideration. Jake had staked out the yes side mostly to annoy Francisco, who kept insisting that a chatbot was "a very confident parrot with a typing habit," and the class had grown so obstreperous that Mr. Lavoie had instituted a talking stick, which was actually a broken metre stick, and which everyone ignored.

Jake's problem was that his side was losing anyway. He had data, heaps of it. He had an article about neural networks detecting damage to their own sensors, a survey of computer scientists, a quote from a sci-fi author he'd found at two in the morning. He had stacked all of it into a persuasive essay due Friday, and when Mr. Lavoie handed back the draft with a single comment in red pen, the comment was "So what?" Which felt, Jake thought, unnecessarily violent for two words.

At lunch he found Veronika in the empty classroom, eating yogurt over her own marked-up essay. She had gotten the same comment. "My evidence is fine," she said, jabbing her spoon at the pages. "Every fact checks out. He circled my whole third paragraph and wrote 'missing link.'" She pulled a library book out of her bag, a fat one with a cracked spine, and turned it toward him. "I found this guy. Stephen Toulmin, 1958, The Uses of Argument. He says an argument has a backbone: a claim, the grounds supporting it, and a warrant."

"What's a warrant?" Jake said.

"The part that explains why your grounds actually support your claim." She tapped the page. "My essay claims the school should cut light pollution. My grounds are page after page of bird migration data. But I never wrote the bit that connects them. Why does disrupting birds mean the school should act? I just assumed everyone could leap the gap with me."

Jake sat down across from her and copied the three words into his notebook: claim, grounds, warrant. Then, because he was honest with himself on good days, he flipped open his own draft and looked for the gap. His essay claimed the artificial mind deserved moral consideration. His grounds were the self-damage-detection article. Between them, nothing. He had proven that the network could sense harm, and then he had simply invited the reader to believe that sensing harm was the same as mattering, that whatever flickered inside it amounted to sentience, and he had never once said so out loud. He had begged the question so smoothly it had beguiled even him.

That night he wrote Veronika a message, because saying it in person meant watching her face, and her face was merciless. "I owe you half my essay. Toulmin's warrant is the bridge, but here's my problem: the bridge has to be built out of something. If I claim the network matters because it can suffer, someone will ask what suffering is, and I don't have that. If I claim it matters because it acts like it suffers, that's Francisco's parrot argument wearing a nicer coat. So maybe the honest move is a conditional. If suffering is the line, and if the network crosses it, then it matters, and the real fight is about whether it crosses it, not about whether crossing it counts. That's a smaller, uglier claim. It might also be a true one. Can I cite your book? Also your yogurt is still in the classroom fridge, I moved it before third period, you're welcome."

Her reply came in four minutes: "Cite the book not me. The conditional thing is good but you have to actually defend the second 'if' or you've just hidden the gap inside a smaller gap. Like nesting dolls of evasion." Then: "Thanks for the yogurt."

On Friday, Jake read his revised essay aloud, and it went about as well as a smaller, uglier claim ever goes. Francisco hammered him on the second if, the what-counts-as-suffering if, and Jake had to say, more than once, "I don't know, that's the part I can't settle," which in a debate round sounds like drowning. Mr. Lavoie wrote something in his binder and didn't share it. Veronika, who had argued the lights-out side of her own paper with the migration data and a warrant about institutional responsibility, got a round of applause, mostly from the two girls on the environmental committee.

After class, though, Mr. Lavoie stopped Jake at the door and said the comment on his draft had been written before anyone turned anything in, the same two words copied onto eleven papers, because in fifteen years of teaching he had found that most students would rather fight a red pen than look for their own missing link. Then he handed back a late draft from Francisco, untouched except for the margin, where the coach of the confident-parrot argument read, in the same red ink, the same two words: So what?

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The standard tuning note is A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 16.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and old carpet, and by August it had become the place where three boys who barely qualified as a band could be loud without anybody calling the police. Deklan's drums lived against the wall beside the deep freezer, Emmanuel's keyboard balanced on two sawhorses, and Chase had his father's guitar, a loaner with strings so dead they had gone the color of tarnished brass. What Chase wanted, with a want that kept him awake some nights, was to be ready by September, when the community center's open rehearsal took anyone who could tune up and play three chords without apology.

The problem was the tuning itself. His father's old clip-on tuner had a cracked screen, so Chase used a phone app, and at first he trusted it the way you trust a thermometer. Then came the evening Emmanuel brought sheet music from his piano teacher, Ms. Xu, who ran the community center ensemble and had told him, in her dry way, that the group tuned together before anything else, one note from a tuner app, no exceptions. Emmanuel passed the music across the keyboard like a secret document. "She said if we can't match her note, we stand at the back."

So they tried. Deklan thumped a beat out of boredom while Chase plucked the open strings and chased the needle, and the app kept telling him he was flat when his ears told him he was fine. He rechecked twice, sweating in the garage heat, until Deklan leaned over his shoulder and started laughing with the virulent delight of someone who has caught a friend in a technical crime. "Dude. Your app's set to 442."

Chase looked. In the settings, buried under menu after menu, the reference frequency read 442 hertz. He had never touched it; the app had simply arrived that way, or he had swiped something wrong months ago, and every session in the garage had been tuned to a note slightly sharper than everyone else's. Emmanuel, who read instruction manuals for pleasure, delivered the correction like a weather report. "The standard is A above middle C at 440 hertz. It's formalized by the International Organization for Standardization." He tapped the page. "ISO 16. That's what it's called."

Chase changed the number and retuned, and the guitar sounded, if anything, slightly worse to him, duller, like it had lost a shimmer he hadn't known he was enjoying. That was the part he hadn't expected: being wrong had sounded good in his garage. He sat with the instrument on his knee and thought about how a week ago he would have argued with the app, or with Ms. Xu, or with the whole idea that a committee somewhere got to decide what an A was. It coagulated in him slowly, the suspicion that the standard wasn't about rightness so much as agreement, and that agreement might matter more.

"What's it even mean," Deklan said, spinning a stick, "that a note is standard? Who decided?" Emmanuel shrugged. "Organizations. Conferences. Old men in rooms." Chase said, "I used to think that was stupid. Like, sound is sound." He picked the retuned string and let it ring against the freezer's hum. "But if we show up at forty-fourity-two and the whole ensemble's at four-forty, we're not slightly wrong, we're wrong together and still alone." Deklan said that was the most emo sentence ever spoken in his garage, and Chase let it go, because it probably was.

At the rehearsal the following Tuesday, Ms. Xu stood at the front of the community center room and held up her phone, and a single thin A filled the space. Chase tuned to it in under a minute, matched string for string, and when he glanced up she was watching him with the mild attention of someone cataloguing who had practiced. He wanted to tell her about the 442, to confess the whole sharpened summer, but there was no slot in the evening for confessions, only the count-in, her raised hand, four silent beats.

He still wasn't sure the standard A was more beautiful than the one he'd been playing all along. He suspected it wasn't, that beauty had nothing to do with committees, and that this didn't change anything. When the ensemble reached the second verse, Ms. Xu cut them off, pointed at Chase, and said, "Again, and this time listen left, not just to yourself." He played the passage again, and this time he could hear Emmanuel's keyboard underneath him, and he followed it.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Agatha Christie's 1926 novel The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, the narrator, Dr Sheppard, turns out to be the murderer.
story:
Rosalie arrived at the library meeting room early, before anyone else, and claimed the chair nearest the window so she could see the parking lot. The book club had six members this term, and she was the youngest by at least thirty years, which meant she had to be careful about how she argued. She had finished The Murder of Roger Ackroyd two days ago, staying up past midnight in her room with the lamp angled away from the door, and she had not seen it coming.

The others arrived in a slow procession: Mr. Yoon, who lived on her street and had recommended the book to her in the first place, then Alysha from her English class, who had come only because Rosalie had begged her, then a woman everyone called the retired postmistress, who talked more than anyone. Paul came last, shaking rain off his jacket, holding a battered copy with a cracked spine and a pencil wedged in it like a bookmark.

"I want to talk about the ending," Rosalie said, once the woman who ran the club had poured the coffee from the thermos. "But first I want to say what I got wrong."

Alysha looked up from her copy, which was still on page forty. "Wrong how?"

"I trusted him." Rosalie laid her palm flat on the cover. "The whole way through. Dr Sheppard, the narrator. I thought he was just this fussy small-town doctor who liked his sister and his vegetables. And then." She stopped, aware that Alysha hadn't finished, aware that spoiling it was a kind of theft. "Have you read it?"

"Tell me anyway," Alysha said. "I'm not going to get to it before next month, honestly."

Rosalie turned the book over in her hands. "The narrator turns out to be the murderer. Dr Sheppard, the man telling us everything, he did it. The book came out in 1926 and people were furious about it, Mr. Yoon told me, because they felt cheated. And I did feel cheated. For about an hour. And then I started thinking that maybe being cheated was the point."

The retired postmistress set down her cup with a small ceramic click. "In my day we didn't blame the storyteller for our own carelessness."

"Maybe not," Rosalie said. "But it's more than that. Because he never exactly lies to us. He just tells us what he does and leaves out what it means. He says he came home and did something he'd rather not describe, and you ascribe it to grief or shock, some normal thing, because that's what a narrator is for. You hand him your trust the way you hand a coat to someone at a door." She heard herself speaking faster and slowed down. "That's what I want to learn to see. How the telling shapes what I believe."

Paul had been flipping through his cracked copy with the pencil, and now he leaned forward. "I've read it three times," he said. "The second time, I went back to the opening chapters to find where he was hiding the truth, and it's all right there. He practically tells you in the first chapter, in this sly way, and then relies on you not to hear it."

"Show us," Rosalie said.

He found the page and read a few lines aloud, and Rosalie listened with her arms folded on the table, and the room went quiet except for the radiator ticking and a trolley of returns squeaking past in the corridor outside. He was right. The confession was there in the shape of a joke, the narrator promising to keep back just enough, and the first-time reader laughed and moved on. She had laughed and moved on.

"There's a kid in my history class," Alysha said, chewing the end of her pen, "who does the same thing. He tells you these stories about why he got detention and they're all technically true and all completely slanted, and by the end you're on his side. I never thought of it as a technique."

"It's a technique," Rosalie said. "Or it's a character. Or both, and that's the part I can't decide." She glanced at Mr. Yoon, who was watching her with his hands folded, and she suspected he had known the ending all along when he handed her the book. "If Sheppard is just a puzzle mechanism, then the book is a trick, a good one but a trick. If he's a person, then the whole novel is a portrait of someone rationalizing, and the reader who trusted him isn't a fool, she's just someone who gives people the benefit of the doubt. And I don't know which one I read. I might not ever know."

The leader of the club said something about dessert, and the retired postmistress began an anecdote about a libel case from 1979 that was, Rosalie admitted privately, evanescent in her memory almost as she heard it, sliding away like the steam off the coffee cups. Alysha pulled her copy of the novel closer and opened it to the first chapter. "I'm going to read it now," she said. "Knowing. I want to see if I catch him."

"You won't," Paul said. "Not because you're not smart. Because knowing isn't the same as not trusting."

Alysha read the first page in silence, and her eyebrows went up. "He's charming," she said. "Why is he so charming?"

Rosalie looked down at her own copy, at the bland, agreeable face of the man on the page, and realized she still liked him, murderer and all.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
The video arrived at 7:14 in the morning, and by second period half the sophomore class had seen it. It showed a flooded street, a man on a roof holding a handwritten sign, water the color of milky tea moving fast below him. Gary had sent it to the group chat with three exclamation points and the words this is happening right now two towns over. Jesse watched it twice in the hallway outside Mr. López's room, his thumb hovering over the share arrow.

Maxim leaned against the lockers beside him, bag strap twisted across his chest. "Are you forwarding it?"

"I don't know." Jesse turned the phone sideways. "My aunt lives near Hillsdale. If this is real, somebody should know."

"Then send it."

But the video bothered him in a way he couldn't locate, the way a word looks wrong on a page even when it's spelled correctly. There was no sound. The light was strange, autumn-low for something filmed in May. He'd learned in Mr. López's media unit that a clip with no source was like a quote with no speaker, and Mr. López had said it plainly enough that it stuck: a responsible person verifies before they amplify. Jesse had nodded at the time the way students nod at principles they assume they'll never need. Now the principle stood in the hallway wearing Gary's handwriting.

"You know what's funny," Maxim said, scrolling on his own phone. "My cousin had this whole thing last year. Some breaking photo everybody was passing around, and it turned out to be years old. He ran it through a reverse image search and found the original." He shrugged. "I think it was TinEye. Some site like that."

"A reverse image search," Jesse repeated. He typed it into the browser, one-handed, pulse quicker than the situation deserved. TinEye loaded, plain and gray, nothing viral about it. He uploaded a still frame from the video, the one with the sign, cropped and shaking.

The screen filled with rows of thumbnails. Jesse's stomach dropped before his mind caught up, because there were dozens of results, and the dates ran back years, not hours. Then he saw the toolbar at the top of the results, a dropdown reading sort by, and beneath it an option: oldest first. He chose it. The page reshuffled itself, and the earliest match surfaced at the head of the list, posted long before this morning, long before this week. Whatever the flood in the video was, it had already happened, had already been photographed, had already circled the internet at least once and come around again dressed as news.

"Send it to Gary," Maxim said quietly. A knot of students had gathered near the doors, phones out, someone saying they were cancelling afternoon practice because of the water.

Jesse typed, deleted, typed again. It was a small thing to correct a group chat, smaller than the flood had felt ten minutes ago, and yet he could feel the pull the other way, the warm certainty of being first with bad news. He thought of his aunt, who was fine, whose street was dry, and of how easily he'd nearly expropriated an old disaster and handed it to sixty people as their own emergency. It seemed like happenstance that Maxim had mentioned his cousin at all, though maybe it wasn't; maybe that was what friends were for, saying the useful thing without knowing it was useful.

He sent the link with the oldest result attached and wrote, not a judgment, just the evidence: this footage is from years ago. The typing dots appeared under Gary's name, disappeared, appeared again. Down the hall, a boy Jesse didn't know held up his phone and said, "Look at this, it's all over everything." Jesse watched his own message land, the little word delivered beneath it, and waited, thumb still, for the typing to stop.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Chicago style offers two citation systems: notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities, and author-date, common in the sciences.
story:
The paper came back on a Tuesday, and Austin read the grade in the hallway before he even reached his locker: a C-minus in blue ink at the top of the first page, and beneath it, in Ms. Iyer's small precise hand, one sentence. "See me. Your citations are in the wrong system." He turned the pages over on the kitchen table that evening, after his mother had gone to her shift, and found the margins flagged all the way down. He had done everything, he thought. Thirty-one footnotes. A bibliography alphabetized twice because the first time he had missed a Cooper source he'd found late. An actual argument, not just a report: that the plow had done more than the sword to end the open range, and he'd proven it, or tried to.

Cooper had told him Chicago style was easy. "Just numbers at the bottom," Cooper had said a month ago, leaning across the lab bench they shared in chemistry. "Number in the text, full citation in the note. It's the lazy person's system." Austin had taken that as fact, the way he took most of what Cooper said, and had formatted his paper accordingly, learning it from the library website at ten at night with a mug of tea going cold beside the keyboard. Now he sat at the kitchen table with the graded pages fanned out in front of him, wondering what a system could even be wrong about. The numbers were there. The notes were there. The bibliography was there. It was like being told he'd driven on the wrong road when the car was parked in the driveway.

He found Ms. Iyer the next morning before the first bell, and she didn't lecture him, which somehow made it worse. She set the paper on her desk and turned to a page. "You used notes, but in the sciences we'd expect the other one." He must have looked blank, because she almost smiled. "Look it up. Tell me tomorrow what you find." He walked to first period feeling like she'd handed him a riddle instead of a correction, and the feeling followed him all day, a small itch under his collar.

At lunch he and Damion crowded a laptop in the library, Damion eating chips over the keyboard in a way that made Austin wince. The style guide's page loaded slowly, the little spinning circle interminable, and then there it was, plain as a street sign. Chicago style offered two systems. One was called notes and bibliography, which was what he'd used, common in history and the humanities. The other was called author-date, common in the sciences. Austin read the line twice. "Wait," he said. "So I did the right style. I just did it in the wrong field." Damion crunched and considered. "So it's not wrong, it's just for somebody else." Austin copied the page into his notebook, and under it wrote a question he didn't have an answer to yet: if the facts are identical, why does it matter whose shelf they're filed on?

He worked at the kitchen table that night, the same spot, the same lamp, but the paper felt different now. He made himself a deal: he would rewrite every citation in author-date, because Ms. Iyer's course was a science course and she'd asked for it, and the rules of a discipline were part of the discipline, like the baseline was part of tennis. But he kept the original draft in a separate folder, and he kept his footnote habit in his head, because he'd discovered he liked notes, the way they let a page breathe, the small numbered asides waiting below like a second conversation. He couldn't have said which was better. Maybe neither was. Maybe the two systems were like two witnesses to the same event, each accurate, each telling it for a different courtroom.

It took him three evenings. In-text citations replaced his numbers; the bibliography became a reference list; a date moved from the end of each entry to just after the author's name, like a name tag worn on the front instead of the back. He noticed, somewhere in the second evening, that he was rewriting sentences too, tightening claims the new format made flabby, and that felt like cheating until he decided it was probably the point. His mother came through on her break, looked at the spread of pages and pencils and the cold mug, and asked if he was winning. "I don't know," he said. "I'm learning the rules of the game I'm actually in."

On Thursday he laid the revised paper on Ms. Iyer's desk and, beside it, one paragraph on a separate sheet: his answer to her riddle, ending with the question he still couldn't settle, whether the form of a citation was mere convention or whether it shaped how a reader trusted the claim. She read it standing up, pen uncapped, and Austin watched her eyes move down the page the way he watched the clock during interminable quizzes, measuring without wanting to be caught measuring. She marked nothing. She looked at him over the sheet.

"You used both, in the end," she said. "The format for me, the question for yourself." Austin shrugged, though something in his chest had gone quiet and warm. She handed the paper back with a note paper-clipped to it, and he didn't read the note until he was alone in the stairwell, where he stood in the noise of departing buses and unfolded it slowly, twice, along its crease.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Denmark, Norway and Sweden have no statutory national minimum wage; pay floors are instead set through collective agreements between unions and employers.
story:
The notice board by the warehouse time clock had been empty all summer except for the safety posters and a faded flyer about the company picnic, so when the union notice went up on Friday, a small crowd formed around it before the six a.m. shift. Brandon stood at the edge of the group, his badge still clipped crooked to his hoodie, and read the words twice. Negotiations. Collective bargaining. Proposed changes to weekend premiums and the scheduling of minors. His supervisor, a broad man named only ever by his last name, cleared his throat and said the company would answer formally, and the crowd dispersed slowly, like people leaving a funeral they weren't sure was over.

Brandon had started at the warehouse in June, three weeks after his seventeenth birthday, unloading trailers and scanning totes for nine dollars an hour with no premium for Saturdays. His mother had signed the permission slip for minors without reading it, the way she signed most things now. The money was for the gap between his scholarship and what college actually cost, a gap he preferred not to think about directly, the way you don't look down from a high place.

That afternoon he sat in the library with Brianna and Krish, preparing for the debate Ms. Vu had assigned them on raising the minimum wage. Brianna had a folder of statistics and the confidence of someone who had already won the argument in her head. Krish kept tilting his chair backward, which was his way of thinking. Brandon was supposed to argue against a raise, a position he didn't hold, and Ms. Vu had told him only that the strongest case is the one you can't dismiss. She never explained anything; she just wrote questions in the margins of his drafts, and he had learned, slowly, to internalize the habit of asking them of himself.

"Here's something," Krish said, tilting forward suddenly, his phone flat on the table between them. "My cousin did a paper on this. Denmark, Norway, Sweden. No national minimum wage. Not in law at all."

"That can't be right," Brianna said. "Those are like the highest-wage countries in the world."

"Look it up." He slid the phone across. Brandon read the screen, then read it again, and felt something rearrange itself in his mind, a wall turning out to be a door. The pay floors in those countries were set through collective agreements between unions and employers, agreement by agreement, industry by industry, without any statute behind them. He copied it into his notes word for word, because in a debate every word would be checked.

He thought of the notice board. He had assumed the union was just part of the furniture of the place, the way the safety posters were, something that existed for other people, in other decades. His grandfather had carried a card for thirty years at the plant in Gary, and had once described the old jurisdictional fights between rival unions as sectarian, almost religious in their bitterness, men who agreed about everything except which door they walked through. Brandon had been eleven, sitting on the porch steps, and had not known the word, only the tone.

On Monday the union rep was back, a small woman with a clipboard, standing near the loading dock where the forklifts came and went. Brandon heard her talking to two of the older pickers about the weekend premium, how the company wanted it gone and the bargaining team wanted it doubled, how everything came down to what they could hold together at the table. One of the pickers, a man Brandon unloaded trailers with, said the new hires wouldn't back it because they didn't stay long enough to care. Then the man turned and looked directly at Brandon, who was by far the youngest person in earshot, and said, "That includes you, college boy. You planning to care?"

"I get Saturdays," Brandon said. "No premium. I didn't know that was on the table."

"It's all on the table," the rep said. "That's the whole point of a table."

At the next debate practice, Brandon laid out his case, and it came out different from what he had planned. He conceded the strongest argument for a raise, then argued that a law was one instrument among several, and that in Denmark and Norway and Sweden there was no statutory national minimum wage at all, because pay floors there were set through collective agreements between unions and employers. Brianna frowned at her folder. Ms. Vu wrote something in the margin of her own notes, which Brandon could not read, and asked only, "And what makes an agreement strong?" He didn't have an answer yet, and said so, and she nodded as if that were the assignment.

He stayed late the following Saturday, unloading a late trailer, and on the way out he stopped at the notice board. The company had posted its formal response, and beneath it the union had posted theirs, and someone had written in pen across the bottom of the union's sheet: meeting Thursday, all shifts, new hires especially. Brandon took out his phone and photographed it, then stood there a moment in the noise of the dock doors rolling down. He didn't know yet whether he would still be working here when any of it was settled, or whether a Thursday meeting was his business at all. He looked at the photo again, put the phone in his pocket, and signed his name on the sheet that was taped beside the flyer.

"See you Thursday, college boy," the picker called from the dock, and raised his coffee cup.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
Raphael arrived at the mall fountain eleven minutes early, which he decided was the correct amount of early, enough to seem eager but not desperate. He had ironed the grey shirt his mother called his interview shirt, and he had rehearsed, on the drive over, three separate openings in case the conversation stalled. Across from him a toddler threw a penny into the water while her father scrolled his phone, and the fountain's noise was steady and low, like rain on a tarp.

Liliana came down the escalator with her jacket unzipped over a swim team hoodie. They had been in the same English class since sophomore year, trading marginal notes in used paperbacks, and he had wanted this for months without ever saying so in plain words. "You found it," she said. "I always get lost past the shoe stores."

"Nickolas drew me a map," Raphael admitted, producing the napkin on which his friend had sketched the mall in blocky ink, the fountain circled twice. "He's a pundit about malls. Thinks he knows everything."

They walked. The plan was the arcade, then food, then whatever. At the counter he paid for the tokens before she could reach for her wallet, and she let him, and that small transaction felt like a treaty signed between two careful governments. They played air hockey and she beat him twice, laughing at his competitive hunch over the table. He found that he did not mind losing, which surprised him, because with Nickolas he minded enormously.

They ended up in the photo booth because the arcade was closing, cramming shoulder to shoulder behind the curtain while the machine counted down from five. On the second flash she turned and kissed him, quick and warm, and he kissed her back, and the booth took their picture mid-motion, so that later the strip would show two people who looked startled and pleased at once. Outside the curtain, catching their breath, he put his hand on her waist, the way he had seen done in a hundred films, and she kept walking beside him with it there toward the exit doors, the evening mall light going amber against the glass.

It was in the parking lot, halfway to her car, that she slowed. "Hey," she said. "Can I say something weird?"

"You can say anything."

"I liked the kiss. I did." She was looking at the pavement, then up at him. "But I'd rather just say goodnight here, if that's okay. The rest of it, the hand, I'm not feeling it tonight. Maybe another night, maybe not. I don't totally know."

Raphael took his hand back and stepped a half-step to give her air, and inside his chest two voices began arguing at once. The first, which sounded like the comment sections he scrolled at two in the morning, insisted that a kiss meant the evening had a direction, that pulling back now was a mixed signal, unfair even. The second, quieter, reminded him of the ninth-grade health unit he'd half-listened to, the part Mr. Paquette had made them repeat until the words stopped sounding strange: consent can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given. At eighteen he finally understood it was not a technicality but the whole point. Yes could become no mid-sentence, mid-evening, mid-kiss, and the no carried the day entirely. Anything else was arithmetic with someone else's body.

"It's okay," he said, and found he meant it, though something in him was still recalculating. "Goodnight sounds good."

She exhaled, and he hadn't realized she'd been holding anything until he saw it leave her. "You're not mad."

"I'm a little disappointed," he said, because honesty seemed owed after a kiss. "But not mad. Those aren't the same thing." She smiled at that, the same crooked smile she aimed at overwrought metaphors in their paperbacks.

She drove away first. He sat in his own car for a while with the photo strip on the passenger seat, four frames of blurred happiness, and tried to decide what he actually knew. That he liked her. That she liked him enough to kiss him and brave enough to stop. That whether there would be a second date was an open question and would stay open, and that he could live inside an open question, which struck him as a more useful skill than anything the arcade had tested. His grandmother, convalescing slowly at his aunt's house after the fall, liked to say that patience was the one thing youth refused to learn; he had always filed this under the category of things adults claim. Sitting there, he texted Nickolas a photo of the photo strip, then deleted it unsent, keeping the evening to himself a while longer. The mall lights behind him went out in sections, one wing at a time, like someone closing a very large book.

He turned the key and pulled out of the space.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
The party had reached the stage where the music was off, the cake was a smear of frosting on twelve plates, and Sebastian was standing on the coffee table with his guitar.

"I wrote this Tuesday," Sebastian announced, which was already a bad sign, since Tuesday was also the day he'd eaten an entire jar of pickled jalapeños on a dare. "It's called 'Pluto Never Left.' It's about how Pluto never left."

"You have one fan," said Maira, raising her cup of punch. "It's me. I'm the fan."

Isaac sat on the floor with his back against the couch and felt the specific dread of a friend about to perform. Sebastian strummed, opened his mouth, and sang. The chords were fine. The melody wandered like it had lost its keys somewhere in the second verse. And the lyrics, which were meant to be tender, contained the phrase "gravitational hug," which made Maira snort punch through her nose.

It went on for four minutes. Isaac spent them recalibrating his face between polite attention and honest horror, and he knew, by the end, that Sebastian would jump down off that table and say, "So? Be honest. I can take it." Sebastian always said that. And Isaac always said "it was good," which was a reprieve for both of them, a short one, and then Sebastian kept writing the same wandering song with the same gravitational hugs, and Isaac kept feeling worse about it.

Sure enough: "So? Be honest. I can take it. Punch me in the face with the truth."

"Your face doesn't need more punching," Maira said, offering him a napkin for the punch on his shirt.

Isaac opened his mouth to say it was good, and then, because he was sixteen and tired of lying to someone he actually liked, he said nothing, which Sebastian correctly read as an answer.

"That bad."

"No. The chords are, like, genuinely good. The bridge is good. The rest of it..."

"Go on." Sebastian sat down on the table's edge, guitar across his knees, and waited, chin up, the way someone waits for a shot at the dentist.

The trouble, Isaac thought, was that he had two ideas fighting in him, and he'd never made them sit down together. One was his mother's rule: if you can't say something nice, say nothing, which protected everyone and improved nothing. The other was the coach's rule from track: honest feedback is a gift, which was true but felt, in practice, like handing someone a box with a wasp in it. Both rules seemed right. Both seemed to leave Sebastian exactly where he was, hugging Pluto.

Then he remembered something. Mr. Kobayashi, who taught across the hall from Isaac's English class, had told them about a study once, not in a lecture, just in passing while handing back essays that bled red ink. In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students revised their essays more when the harsh comments came stapled to a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them. Not softer comments. The same comments, plus one sentence of belief.

"When Mr. Kobayashi handed back our essays," Isaac said slowly, "he put a sticky note on mine. It said, 'This is a rough draft of something better than you think.' And it worked. I actually revised it. There was this study he told us about, 2014, David Yeager, and the students who got the belief note revised way more than the ones who just got the criticism."

"That's diabolical," Maira said, delighted.

"It's not a trick," Isaac said. "It's only a trick if the belief part is fake."

Sebastian eyed him. "So you're stalling before you insult my song by telling me you believe in me first."

"Sort of. But here's the thing, I actually do. The bridge is the best thing you've written. If the whole song were the bridge, I'd want it on my phone."

Sebastian blinked. Maira, who had been rotating a cake fork like a tiny baton, stopped rotating it.

"The bridge," Sebastian said.

"The bridge works because the melody stays put for once. The verses wander, like they're looking for a parking space. And 'gravitational hug'..."

"Don't."

"I'm not going to apologize for 'gravitational hug.' It's a virulent phrase. It spread through my brain all week and now Maira has it too."

"It's true," Maira said solemnly. "I've had it since Tuesday."

Sebastian looked down at his guitar and picked out the bridge, softly, the one part where everything Isaac had said was true. He played it twice. Then he played the verse after it, but changed, anchored, and something in Isaac's chest went loose with relief.

"Okay," Sebastian said. "But you have to understand I'm going to sing it at the winter showcase, and if it fails in front of three hundred people, that's on you and your sticky note science."

"Deal," said Isaac, and then, because honesty was apparently a door that swung both ways, "I don't actually know if it'll work on songs. The study was essays. It might only work on essays."

Sebastian considered this, strummed a chord, and grinned. "Then we're about to run the experiment."

Maira raised her cup again. "To Pluto, which never left, and to 'gravitational hug,' which also never leaves."

"Stop," said Sebastian, and started the song from the top.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The Cochranes' basement smelled like nacho cheese and wet umbrellas, because Mr. Castillo had insisted everyone come to his place for the AFC championship even though his television was only slightly bigger than Noemie's phone propped against a book. Noemie sat on the carpet between Hailie and Lyra, holding a bowl she wasn't eating from, while the younger kids sprawled closer to the screen. There was the quarterback, there the roaring crowd, and there, stretched across the grass like a ribbon someone had laid down for a party, the yellow line.

"Coach said the refs repaint it every first down," said Teo, the seven-year-old who belonged to somebody upstairs. "With a machine."

Noemie looked at the line. Then she looked at the players' shoes, which crossed it and uncrossed it constantly without smudging it, without leaving a single green streak or footprint or disturbance of any kind. The line lay under the players, in fact, not on them; when a receiver stepped across it, his cleats covered the yellow, and then it reappeared around his ankles like water closing over a stone. Paint did not behave that way. Paint did not have opinions about cleats.

"That's not paint," she said.

"It is," Teo said. "It's yellow paint."

"Watch," she said, and she pointed. "Watch his foot. See how the line goes behind him?" Teo watched. His mouth opened slightly, the way a mouth does when the floor tilts.

Lyra leaned over, interested in spite of herself. Lyra claimed to find football boring, a position she maintained while never once leaving the room during a game. "So what is it, then?" she asked. "Some kind of projection?"

Noemie didn't know. That was the part she liked, actually: not knowing, and being in a basement full of people who might. She turned the question over the way she turned over most questions, feeling for the edges of it. If it wasn't paint and it wasn't a light shining on the field, then it had to be added afterward, somewhere between the field and the screen, which meant it lived only in the broadcast, a stratum laid over the image for people at home. The seventy thousand people in the stadium were watching a field with no line on it at all. The whole country was seeing something that, in the physical world, did not exist.

Mr. Castillo came down with a tray of celery nobody would touch, and Noemie asked him, and he lit up the way he always did when anyone under twenty asked him anything genuine. He had read about it once, he said, in some magazine he couldn't name. The yellow first-down line was drawn by a computer, and the first broadcast with it had been on ESPN, on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision. He said "Sportvision" the way you'd say the name of a band you'd loved in high school, slightly embarrassed and slightly proud.

"A company called Sportvision," Teo repeated, tasting the words. "Like it's their line."

"It is their line," Hailie said. "It's theirs and it's fake and it's the only reason any of us knows what a first down is." Hailie's father was a statistician and she had inherited his habit of trenchant pronouncements, delivered as though further discussion were optional. Noemie privately thought further discussion was never optional, but she let it sit.

The game went on. A running back crossed the yellow line, or crossed the place where the yellow line only appeared to be, and the crowd roared, and Teo cheered with total commitment to an event he now understood was partly invented. Noemie tried to metabolize the two things at once: that the line was not real, and that it told the truth. The line was more accurate than paint would have been, more accurate than a chain crew marching out to measure with actual metal poles, or at least faster, and yet nobody on the field could see it. She could not decide whether that made television honest or dishonest, and she suspected the question was badly formed, and she suspected she'd keep turning it over on the walk home regardless.

"Okay," Teo said, scooting backward into her lap without asking, the way small children treat older girls as furniture. "So is the end zone real?"

"Completely real," Noemie said. "That part they actually paint."

Teo considered this, then pointed at the screen. "Then why is the yellow line better than the real paint?"

The quarterback took the snap, dropped back, and threw the ball low and hard toward the marker that only they could see, and the whole basement came up off the carpet at once, celery tray tipping, somebody's soda rolling, Teo screaming with his hands in the air.
